title: Pitch perfect cultural diplomacy wins heart of China’s first lady Peng Liyuan
content:
Pitch perfect cultural diplomacy wins heart of China’s first lady Peng Liyuan
Young singers’ rendition of beloved folk song ‘Jasmine Flower’ evokes warm reaction from the renowned soprano during Smithsonian visit
Footage shows the Hope Chinese School youth choir waving Chinese and American national flags during their rendition of the song “Jasmine Flower”, while Peng watches with a smile, her lips moving along to the lyrics.
As the performance ends, she turns to her US counterpart and smiles, while placing a hand to her heart, visibly moved. The two first ladies applaud the children, with Peng calling out “bravo”.
The iconic Chinese folk song, also known as “Mo Li Hua”, has long been part of Peng’s repertoire.
As a celebrated soprano with the People’s Liberation Army, she has sung it on numerous major occasions, including the 2008 Beijing Olympics one-year countdown celebration at Tiananmen Square.

title: Funny Texas nursing home bros from ‘Builder’s Club,’ assembling furniture for people in need
content:
Few things in life are harder than assembling a piece of furniture right out of the box. A group of selfless men with tons of patience and handyman skills at Legacy Oaks of Midlothian in Midlothian, Texas, however, are helping their community do just that—all while bringing lots of laughs.
Together, the five-man team formed the Builder’s Club to help fellow residents and community members assemble furniture for free. News of the rowdy crew spread quickly after a hilarious video was shared on the retirement home‘s Instagram page.
Followers fell in love with their generous hearts—and gentle ribs on each other.
The Builder’s Club goes viral
In the video that has been viewed over 4.5 million times, the Builder’s Club made its internet debut.
When one member was asked, “What’s your favorite thing about being in Builder’s Club?” he responded with humor. “It keeps me out of trouble,” he said. Another member quipped that his favorite thing was “watching him trying to stay out of trouble.”
The group is busy putting together a cabinet for a resident “free of charge.”
One member of the Builder’s Club told viewers, “I just enjoy building. That’s the main thing.” Another member added that it “gives me something to hang around with these guys for.”
The Builder’s Club is gifted free tools
In a follow-up video, the Builder’s Club opens a surprise package from two fans, a brother and sister named Brandon and Holly, who were inspired to bless them with brand-new toys to support their building projects.
In a letter, Brandon and Holly shared, “My sister Holly and I saw the video of you guys on Instagram. I was informed you may have some needs to make your job a little easier. We’ve thrown in a few things that might help and hope you can use them to continue your pursuits.”
The guys unbox a “castle of screwdrivers” that has a five-year warranty, which was the perfect lead-in to a good joke: “That’s more warranty than we’ve got! Lifetime guarantee!”
Another joked, “I’ll tell you what—put my name on the one with the battery!”
How the Builder’s Club got started
The Builder’s Club began in 2024 after a complicated request: a resident needed help building a complex Christmas toy. Since then, the group has built “everything from Target cash registers and motorized ride-on vehicles to patio furniture and staff breakroom lockers.”
Justin Anderson, Executive Director at Legacy Oaks of Midlothian, said in a press release shared with Upworthy, “Depending on the complexity and size of the project, different people at different times will work on it. When we see boxes get delivered and we think they need to be built or assembled, we ask the owner if they want the Builder’s Club to do it for them.”
The Builder’s Club has expanded its outreach to the local Texas community.
“They’ve now built two of those playhouses for residents’ grandchildren, and the kids came to our community to receive them. It’s one of the best things I’ve seen here,” Anderson added.
Viewers respond
Both videos got lots of love from viewers, who hyped up the Builder’s Club:
“These men need protecting at all costs.”
“Builders AND comedians 😂😂😂😂”
“I’d pay for a full season of these guys.”
“I love when the internet actually brings me joy!!! Love this!!!”
“Imagine if they could have a class of five or so youth to teach basic handy skills like this. They could change an entire generation.”
“Those are fellas I would love to hang out with. Btw, we need to keep him out of trouble 😂”
“This is great! All these men have skills from a lifetime of experience and it’s nice that they can keep using those skills! I bet they are a lot of fun too!”
“These gentlemen need to set up outside of a university dorm during move-in day!! ❤️”

title: A Cross-Lingual Acoustic Disease-Alignment Framework for Respiratory Health Assessment from Spontaneous Speech
content: Spontaneous speech offers a scalable, noninvasive signal for respiratory health assessment, yet interpretable models that generalize across languages remain challenging because disease-related acoustic changes are confounded by language-specific phonetic variation. We present CL-DAF, a Cross-Lingual Disease-Alignment Framework that identifies acoustic dimensions whose disease effects remain consistent across languages. Using 201 English and 75 newly collected Bangla speakers, we construct a common 272-dimensional acoustic representation and quantify disease alignment using signed rank-biserial effects and the Language Invariance Score. We first show that spontaneous Bangla speech separates COPD from controls (AUC 0.85); however, 133 features reverse their disease direction across languages and the full representation transfers poorly (AUC 0.49 from Bangla to English). CL-DAF isolates 26 disease-aligned features that raise AUCs to 0.825 and 0.722 from English to Bangla and Bangla to English, respectively. These findings provide a foundation for multilingual clinical speech models emphasizing pathology over language-dependent variation.

title: Can Nepal protect Yomari?
content:
Culture & Lifestyle
Can Nepal protect Yomari?
Why does the country have no legal claim to its own most valuable heritage, and what will it take to build one.Sabina Acharya
Every year, as the month of November-December arrives, the sweet fragrance of steamed rice flour and warm chaku or khuwa fill drifts through the narrow lanes of Bhaktapur, Kathmandu and Lalitpur.
Newa families come together to form small fish-shaped dumplings, known as Yomari, from freshly harvested rice, filled with sesame seeds, coconuts, chaku or khuwa, prepared in a ritual that dates back centuries.
The festival for this food, called Yomari Punhi, is not just a cultural celebration; it is the embodiment of an agricultural knowledge system, linking a particular community, a particular crop, and a particular season.
However, if any foreign food company started producing Yomari today and began labeling it in a supermarket in another country, Nepal would have no legal means to prevent it, as there is no law, no registry, and no enforcement mechanism.
Nepal has 59 officially recognised indigenous nationalities called Adivasi Janajati, comprising around 35 percent of the total population. These span all the ecological zones.
Every community has its own identity, not only in its language and clothing but also in the way it grows its food, prepares its meals, weaves, carves, and heals. Their identity is inseparable from their products.
And yet, while Nepal has precise data on the number of its indigenous communities, it has almost no systematic data on what those communities actually produce.
There is no comprehensive national registry of traditional foods, no catalogue of indigenous medicinal herbs and their community custodians, and no documented inventory of craft techniques and their geographic distribution. Nepal knows it has 59 indigenous nationalities, but it does not know, in any legally useful sense, what those nationalities make, how they make it, or what makes it irreplaceable. A country cannot protect what it has not documented.
Researchers and institutions have identified over 100 agricultural products and 87 potential products that would qualify for international protection as Geographical Indications, a form of intellectual property that protects products whose quality or reputation is tied to a specific geographic origin.
But identification is not documentation. Information about Ilam Tea does not carry the same value as having a legally binding record of its growing altitude, the soil’s characteristics that affect its muscatel taste, and the traditional tea-making processes of the communities who grow it in Ilam. That documentation is required for registration.
For example, compare Yomari with Rasgulla, a centerpiece of one of India’s most famous Geographical Indication disputes, the syrup-soaked cottage cheese ball. The origin of Rasgulla has been disputed for years between West Bengal and Odisha. In 2017, West Bengal was awarded the Geographical Indications status for Banglar Rosogolla, and in 2019, Odisha was awarded the status of GI for Odisha Rasgola, acknowledging the two as separate products from different traditions. Each state’s producers were legally recognised, allowing them to mark their products as authentic, prevent imitations, and establish a market identity tied to their provenance.
Yomari is Nepal’s Rasgulla.
It has a specific community origin, a geographic tie, a centuries-old preparation tradition, and an international diaspora market that already recognises and values it. The difference is that West Bengal and Odisha had a legal system in which to file their claims. Nepal does not.
The same logic applies across Nepal’s entire indigenous product landscape, like Juju Dhau, the King of Yogurt, made in Bhaktapur.
Jumli Marshi rice is grown in Jumla, at an altitude of 2,000-2,900 metres, and depends on the unique flavour and nutritional characteristics of the extreme temperature variations and soil conditions provided by the Karnali region to make it the world’s tallest rice. The weaving density and pattern combinations of Palpali Dhaka fabric are linked to the weaving knowledge tradition practiced by the artisans of Palpa.
Khukuri knives, made by the blacksmith communities in Bhojpur, are known worldwide as a symbol of Nepali craftsmanship due to their curved shape and the steel tempering they undergo. Sherpa, Tamang, and Tibetan Buddhist communities use mineral pigments in a hand-ground technique and iconometric precision to create thangka paintings that are available in international art markets at prices that reflect centuries of value. All these products are potential GI products but are not registered due to the absence of law.
Geographical Indication is the most appropriate legal tool for addressing this. Unlike a patent, it does not require novelty, nor does it require individual authorship as copyright does, nor can it be sold away from the community that owns it, as with a trademark. A GI belongs to all qualified producers in a defined geographic area who meet the production standards.
It is the only form of intellectual property designed for knowledge that is communal, intergenerational, and geographically rooted. And it is the only instrument that connects indigenous communities directly to international markets based on authenticated origin.
The market argument is not abstract. Across international commodity markets, GI-registered products consistently command price premiums over comparable non-registered alternatives. Darjeeling Tea, India’s first GI registration in 2004, commands a price of five to twelve times that of generic Indian black tea in European and Japanese specialty markets.
The Tea Board of India has registered the Darjeeling certification mark in roughly 30 countries. Ilam Tea, grown in ecologically comparable conditions sixty kilometers across the border, is exported to the same markets at a fraction of the price because Nepal has no equivalent certification system.
The farmers of Ilam are not producing an inferior product. They are producing an uncertified one. Nepal’s National Pashmina Sector Export Strategy aims to achieve an export volume of USD75 million in Pashmina by 2026, up from USD15 million in 2023-24.
The goal cannot be accomplished by marketing alone, once the term ‘Pashmina’ has become a generic name for machine-spun blended fiber available in airport stores in Asia and Europe. The only instrument that can restore the word to its authentic meaning and protect that meaning in law is GI registration backed by active enforcement.
This is why the Industrial Property Bill, 2082, introduced to the House of Representatives by the Ministry of Industry, Commerce and Supplies, represents the most significant step Nepal has taken on this issue in its legislative history.
For the first time, the Bill formally recognises Geographical Indications as a distinct and independent category of intellectual property, separated from trademarks, patents, and copyrights. It defines a geographical indication as a sign or geographical name that identifies goods originating from a particular region, where a specific quality, reputation, or characteristic is essentially attributable to that geographical origin.
That definition aligns Nepal, for the first time, with the international standard set by the TRIPS Agreement and with the domestic frameworks of countries that have used GI law to transform indigenous heritage into protected and profitable market assets. The Bill also proposes establishing an Industrial Property Office to administer GI registration and includes provisions to prevent unfair competition and the deceptive use of geographical names.
But the government cannot afford to wait for enactment before beginning the preparatory work that will determine whether the new law has anything meaningful to protect. The most urgent task Nepal faces right now is not legislative. It is documentary. Before a single GI application can be filed, before a single product can be examined and registered, the evidence base must exist.
Geographic boundaries must be mapped. Traditional production methods must be recorded. Community histories of origin must be compiled. Product quality standards must be defined. This work must begin immediately, in parallel with the Bill's parliamentary passage, so that the moment the law creates a registration mechanism, Nepal's producers are ready to use it.
The government must launch a National Traditional Knowledge Documentation Initiative without delay, coordinated across the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, the Ministry of Industry Commerce and Supplies, the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment, the Indigenous Nationalities Commission, and the National Foundation for Development of Indigenous Nationalities and Local Governments. This cannot be the work of one ministry acting alone. It requires field research, community consultation, geographic mapping, agricultural science, and legal analysis to work together systematically across all 59 indigenous nationalities and all ecological zones.
Non-governmental organisations and international NGOs working across Nepal's communities are essential partners in this effort and must be actively mobilised. They are already present in the villages where Dhaka is woven, in the tea gardens where Ilam farmers work, in the high-altitude communities where Yarsagumba is harvested, and in the community where Yomari is traditionally made.
Their field presence, community relationships, and research capacity can reach where government agencies cannot. WIPO’s traditional knowledge documentation guidelines provide a ready methodological framework that NGOs and research institutions can apply immediately. Local governments, empowered under Nepal’s federal structure, must also be formally directed and adequately resourced to participate.
What is needed now is the urgency to act, the coordination to document, and the institutional commitment to implement before the opportunity closes.
The question is not whether Nepal can protect Yomari. It never was. The question is whether Nepal will choose to protect it while there is still time.

title: 단 5마리서 350마리로…멸종위기 새의 기적 같은 부활
content:
AI 추천 뉴스




단 5마리서 350마리로…멸종위기 새의 기적 같은 부활
뉴질랜드 검은 울새
올해의 새로 선정
올해의 새로 선정


전 세계에서 다섯 마리만 남아 멸종 위기에 놓였던 뉴질랜드의 검은 울새 '카루레'가 뉴질랜드 환경보호단체가 선정한 '올해의 새'가 됐다.
뉴질랜드 환경보호단체 '포레스트앤버드'는 지난 21일(현지시간) 카루레가 올해의 새 투표에서 2만5610표를 얻어 1위에 올랐다고 발표했다.
카루레는 뉴질랜드 본토에서 약 800㎞ 떨어진 채텀제도에 서식하는 새로 성체의 무게가 AA 사이즈 건전지 정도에 불과할 만큼 작으며, 주로 숲에서 곤충을 섭취한다.
이 새는 서식지 감소와 외래 포식자의 영향으로 개체 수가 급감해 한때 멸종 직전까지 몰렸다. 1980년에는 단 5마리만 남기도 했다. 당시 암컷 '올드 블루'와 수컷 '올드 옐로' 한 쌍이 사실상 종을 이어갈 마지막 개체였다.
이에 뉴질랜드 당국과 현지 주민은 이들을 보호하고 개체 수를 늘리는 복원 작업에 나섰다. 특히 카루레의 알을 다른 새에게 맡겨 부화시키는 방식 등을 활용해 번식을 유도했다. 이 같은 노력에 힘입어 현재 약 350마리의 카루레 성체가 두 곳의 포식자 차단 자연보호구역에서 서식 중이다.
카루레는 현재도 뉴질랜드에서 '국가적으로 심각한 위기(Nationally Critical)' 단계로 분류되는 등 멸종 위기에서 벗어나지 못했다. 특히 현재 보호구역의 적합한 서식 공간은 거의 포화 상태이기 때문에 개체 수를 더 늘리려면 새로운 서식지를 확보해야 한다.
보전단체들은 채텀제도의 피트섬을 새로운 서식지 후보로 지목했다. 외래 포식자를 제거해 카루레가 번식할 수 있는 환경을 조성하는 것이 목표다. 피트섬 복원은 카루레뿐 아니라 채텀제도에 서식하는 다른 멸종위기 조류를 보호하는 데도 도움이 될 것으로 예상된다.
한편 이번 '올해의 새' 투표에는 역대 최다인 약 10만5000명이 참여했으며, 2위는 카카포, 3위는 뉴질랜드 매인 카레아레아다.

title: Maradi a ses 455 tonnes de fournitures ; reste à les faire parvenir jusqu’au dernier village
content: © Gouvernorat de Maradi Huit jours avant la rentrée du 1er octobre, la région se déclare couverte. Le gouverneur mise désormais sur la vigilance des préfets pour que cahiers et crayons atteignent les écoles les plus éloignées. MARADI, 23 septembre 2026— La région dispose désormais de 455 tonnes de fournitures scolaires, un volume que son gouverneur juge suffisant pour couvrir l’ensemble des besoins de l’année 2026-2027. Le Contrôleur général de police Issoufou Mamane a réceptionné officiellement, mercredi, 360 tonnes livrées par le ministère de l’Éducation nationale ; 95 tonnes conservées de l’an dernier complètent le stock. La cérémonie s’est tenue à la Direction régionale de l’Éducation nationale, de l’Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des Langues (DREN). Autour du gouverneur se tenaient le secrétaire général de la région, AbdoulKarim Mahamadou, son adjoint Maman Lawan Mamane, le directeur régional Amadou Harouna, les cadres du système scolaire et les responsables des forces de défense et de sécurité. Une équation qui tourne à l’avantage de la région Les chiffres avancés par le gouverneur permettent de reconstituer le bilan. Les 360 tonnes reçues correspondent à 85 % des besoins que Maradi avait chiffrés et transmis au ministère. Le manque à combler pesait donc une soixantaine de tonnes ; la réserve de 95 tonnes le dépasse d’une trentaine. Le calcul, pas à pas 360 t ÷ 0,85 ≈ 424 t de besoins exprimés 360 t + 95 t = 455 t disponibles, soit environ 31 t de marge. Estimation de la rédaction, établie à partir des pourcentages et volumes donnés par le gouverneur. Fournitures scolaires : un lot complet pour démarrer l'année Le ministère a répondu à la demande formulée par la région. Le lot se compose surtout de cahiers, d’ensembles géométriques, de stylos à bille, de crayons et de correcteur liquide, autrement dit le nécessaire d’un élève comme d’un enseignant pour bien démarrer. Une réserve héritée de l’an dernier Les 95 tonnes en stock racontent l’histoire d’une première dotation qui avait dépassé la consommation. Selon le gouverneur, l’an dernier, la région avait couvert toute l’année scolaire et mis de côté cet excédent. Il rappelle que l’État nigérien accompagne le monde scolaire depuis 2023 pour alléger la charge des familles et du corps enseignant. Le dernier kilomètre, vrai test de la rentrée Le gouverneur a chargé la direction régionale d’acheminer ces fournitures conformément aux instructions des plus hautes autorités. Son message tient en une idée : chaque cahier doit arriver chez « les vrais destinataires ». Il a annoncé qu’il alerterait les préfets et les administrateurs de villes pour que chacun tienne son rôle, jusque dans les villages les plus reculés. "Rien de ce stock ne doit se retrouver sur les étals des marchés, prévient le gouverneur." — Issoufou Mamane, gouverneur de Maradi La région, a-t-il promis, veillera à ce que ces fournitures, acquises à grands frais, ne fassent pas l’objet d’une revente. Il a aussi remercié le Président de la République, le Premier ministre, les membres du CNSP et le gouvernement pour l’effort consenti. La formation technique dans la tournée Le gouverneur a poursuivi sa journée à la Direction régionale de l’Enseignement et de la Formation techniques et professionnels (DREFTP), où le directeur, Mahamane Manou Mahamane Rabiou, lui a présenté le dispositif mis en place. Passer de l’une à l’autre direction, a-t-il expliqué, montre que l’État n’oublie aucun de ses enfants. Il s’attend à ce que les matières d’œuvre suivent, comme l’an dernier, afin que les apprenants reçoivent une formation adaptée aux besoins du marché. Matières d’œuvre : de quoi parle-t-on ? Ce sont les matériaux consommés pendant les travaux pratiques des filières techniques et professionnelles. Leur arrivée conditionne les cours d’atelier. La rentrée des classes Les classes rouvrent le 1er octobre. D’ici là, la direction régionale doit organiser la répartition, et les préfets relayer la consigne sur le terrain. Le gouverneur a souhaité à toute la communauté scolaire une bonne année et de meilleurs résultats. title: Bewoners van nieuw asielcentrum in Ukkel maken fietstocht om buurt te leren kennen
content:
Tegen het asielcentrum in de Ukkelse Beeckmanstraat kwam heel wat protest. Fietsorganisatie Uccle Avello wil in samenwerking met Samusocial (de uitbater van het centrum) de nieuwe bewoners nu toch op een leuke manier laten kennismaken met de buurt.
Bewoners van nieuw asielcentrum in Ukkel maken fietstocht om buurt te leren kennen
Sinds 15 september komen de eerste asielzoekers aan in het opvangcentrum in Ukkel. Het gaat voornamelijk om gezinnen met kinderen, in totaal zo'n 230 mensen.
Middels een fietstocht willen Samusocial, Uccle Avello en vzw Du haut de mon potager hen leren kennismaken met de buurt op Autoloze Zondag. Er zijn drie fietstochten gepland: om 14 uur, 15.30 uur en 17 uur.
Groepjes van vijf tot acht bewoners worden begeleid door gidsen en maken kennis met verschillende nuttige plekken: scholen, bibliotheken, winkels, parken en het openbaar vervoer. De route loopt onder meer langs het Wolvendaalpark, het Raspailpark en het Heldenplein, zodat de deelnemers vertrouwd kunnen raken met hun nieuwe omgeving. Later zullen er nog cursussen worden georganiseerd voor diegenen die hun fietsvaardigheid in het stadsverkeer willen verbeteren.

title: Plant a Tree Day Origin and History: How Reforestation Grew to New Heights
content:
Our projects focus on restoring priority landscapes around the world—places where forests can make the biggest difference for nature and communities.
Click here to learn about our work
In the fall of 2018, 600 people showed up at 30 different sites — all to do the same thing: dig holes in the ground and put trees in them. By the end of the day, they'd planted more than 7,000 trees and shrubs. It was the very first Plant a Tree Day, and every year since, the event has grown into a global day for reforestation and celebration.
Plant a Tree Day is One Tree Planted’s annual day of action, held every Sept. 28, built to turn awareness of forest loss into planting, volunteering, and giving. It runs as a coordinated push across our network each year, timed to the start of fall planting season in the Northern Hemisphere, when the ground is ready for new roots. It's a day of action — getting new trees in the ground — and it’s also designed to prove that individual efforts can add up to something at landscape scale.
The day has since outgrown its founding numbers. We've now planted more than 171 million trees with 489 partners across 84 countries, and Plant a Tree Day has become the moment each year when we ask people to convert that broader mission into a personal action, whether that's organizing a local planting or giving directly toward reforestation efforts.
Planting in late September is also practical. Fall planting benefits from cooler air, steadier rainfall, and soil that's still warm enough for root growth to continue for weeks after leaves drop, giving new trees a head start before the stress of a hot, dry summer arrives.
We have seen firsthand that collective action scales in a way individual effort can't. A single donation or a single afternoon with a shovel may seem small on its own, but stacked against thousands of other people doing the same thing on the same day, it becomes visible, both to the volunteers themselves and to the partners and municipalities deciding whether reforestation is worth investing in.
The second reason for Plant a Tree Day is more sobering. The UN's Global Forest Goals Report 2026, drawn from voluntary national reports submitted by 48 countries representing 51 percent of the world's forest area, found that global forest area declined by more than 40 million hectares between 2015 and 2025.
The world has lost 420 million hectares of forest since 1990, an area larger than the entire European Union. The rate of loss has eased somewhat, from roughly 16 million hectares a year in the 1990s to about 10 million hectares annually between 2015 and 2020, but primary forest, the old-growth stands that took centuries to form and can't simply be replanted, has shrunk by more than 80 million hectares over the same three decades.
The UN’s own accounting shows progress, but not at the pace 2030 requires. Of the 26 targets tracked under the UN Strategic Plan for Forests, seven are broadly met and 17 are partially achieved, but two are off track entirely: reversing forest loss and eradicating extreme poverty among forest-dependent communities. "As 2030 approaches, the challenge is no longer only to recognize the value of forests but to scale implementation at the speed required," Juliette Biao, director of the United Nations Forum on Forests Secretariat at the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs said in a statement accompanying the report.
Ecosystem services from the world's forests, clean water filtration, flood control, pollination, and soil stabilization among them, are worth an estimated $16.2 trillion annually, with more than 1.6 billion people depending directly on forests for timber, food, fuel, and shelter, according to the UN.
Forests host 80% of the world's amphibian species, 75% of its bird species, and 68% of its mammal species, a concentration that makes forests the backbone of terrestrial life. Standing forests also currently absorb around 30% of the carbon dioxide humans emit each year, acting as one of the planet's largest active carbon sinks.
Shaded surfaces can run 20 to 45 degrees Fahrenheit cooler at peak temperatures than unshaded pavement or roofing, a gap wide enough to meaningfully lower cooling costs and heat-related illness in dense neighborhoods. A single tree can also draw between 10 and 150 gallons of water from the ground on a given day, releasing nearly all of it back into the atmosphere through transpiration and keeping less than 5% for its own growth, which is why tree cover often shows up in flood and drought management plans.
Community-organized events remain the backbone of Plant a Tree Day, and our forest fundraiser platform turns everyday personal milestones into reforestation campaigns, from a birthday, a marathon, or community challenge with the proceeds funneled straight into restoration work.
Donations made through Plant a Tree Day go toward restoring critical habitats and healing landscapes where the need is greatest, rather than being tied to a single, predetermined location. Membership in our Grove monthly giving community offers that same support on a recurring basis, at whatever amount someone chooses to set.
The UN is now pressing governments to support reforestation efforts. "Forests are essential to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals, from climate action and biodiversity conservation to food security and resilient livelihoods," said Bjørg Sandkjær, Assistant Secretary-General for Policy Coordination at the UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs. "Investing in forests is investing in climate stability, resilient economies and the well-being of present and future generations."
At its core, though, Plant a Tree Day is still individuals all around the world, in groups large or small, committed to putting roots in the ground because tree planting is an activity always worthy of an afternoon.
Jill Ettinger is a writer and editor covering the intersection of culture and sustainability. Her reporting connects our everyday choices to the environmental and social-justice stories shaping them, from the products we put in our carts to the communities a changing climate touches most. She is based in Los Angeles.

RESEARCHERS FROM UNIVERSITY of Galway are part of an international team working to restore deep-sea coral reefs damaged by bottom trawling by installing 3D-printed artificial reefs.
The research has seen 23 artificial reefs placed on the deep seabed off the south-west Porcupine Bank, off the west coast of Ireland and in the Bay of Biscay, France.
The early results are said to be “very encouraging” and researchers said the work could “open up new possibilities to scale up the restoration of damaged coral reefs elsewhere in the Atlantic and beyond”.
It’s part of a Horizon Europe project titled ‘REDRESS’, which is an acronym for “Restoration of deep-sea habitats to rebuild European Seas”.
The expedition to deploy the artificial reefs took place last month on board L’Atalante, a vessel of the French Oceanographic Fleet.
Reefs were placed at depths between 900 and 1,100m off the Porcupine Bank, and in the Guilvinec Canyon, Bay of Biscay – other reefs were installed here during an expedition last year too.
While cold-water coral reefs are less well-known than their tropical cousins, they provide important habitats for marine life and support biodiversity in the deep-sea, including fish.
The corals, however, are quite fragile and easily damaged by deep-sea trawling.
While recent fisheries and conservation regulations prohibit trawling in many areas where corals are found, the issue is now turning to how to return damaged areas to full health.
The artificial reefs are eco-designed cylinders made from low-carbon concrete incorporating volcanic material.
Each 3D-printed structure is around 80cm high and 100cm in diameter, weighing around 600kg.
They provide complex physical microhabitats including tunnels, ledges and overhangs, that offer shelter and provide surfaces for corals and other marine life to colonise.
The reefs are placed individually on the seabed, rather than together, to form a single connected structure covering an area of about half a hectare.
Researchers will monitor the sites over the coming years through photography, video and 3D mapping to assess how the coral and other marine life develop on and around the reefs.
Different approaches are also being tested as part of the research.
Some reefs were equipped with oyster shells, ceramic plates and tiles to encourage coral larvae to settle naturally, while others were fitted with fragments of living coral.
The aim is to see whether the coral can survive and establish new colonies or enhance the attractiveness of the artificial reefs for colonisation by coral larvae.
Encouragingly, researchers have found that the coral fragments, known as nubbins, which were placed on artificial reefs last year are still alive.
The reefs have also been colonised by a range of marine species, including sea urchins, fish, crabs and crinoids.
The research will also monitor seawater conditions, sediment and chemical contaminants.
This will help improve understanding of the conditions needed for healthy coral growth and assess the potential impact of climate change and ocean acidification on restoration efforts.
Both restoration sites, meanwhile, are now protected from further damage by bottom trawling.
Dr Anthony Grehan, a deep-sea ecologist at University of Galway and co-leader of the mission to the Porcupine Bank, said these “deep-sea coral reefs provide vital habitat for a diversity of marine life, but many have been damaged over many years”.
“Because these corals grow by only a few millimetres each year, natural recovery of lost reefs can take decades to centuries.
“With this project, we are testing whether we can actively accelerate that recovery by creating new starter structures for corals to grow on, which also mimic reef structure to help re-establish functioning reef habitats.”
Grehan said the “early results are very encouraging” and added: “If we can show that these approaches work, it could open up new possibilities to scale up the restoration of damaged coral reefs elsewhere in the Atlantic and beyond.”
Meanwhile, Marie-Claire Fabri, a research engineer in deep-sea benthic ecology and co-leader of the Bay of Biscay region expedition, remarked that “preserving these areas alone is not enough” and called for the “active restoration of cold-water corals”.
“The ban on bottom trawling has helped stop the direct pressure on these habitats, but to go further – given the slow growth of these corals in the Atlantic – just a few millimetres per year—we cannot simply wait for them to recover on their own.”

title: Solad Accelerates Solar Home System Deployment
content:
Latest Headlines
Solad Accelerates Solar Home System Deployment
Kayode Tokede
Solad is accelerating access to Solar Home Systems across underserved communities in Nigeria as the country enters a new phase in the growth of distributed renewable energy.
Solad has already deployed more than 1,800 Solar Home Systems across five Nigerian states, with a further 4,000 plus earmarked for roll-out.
The programme expands the company’s distributed energy footprint and supports Nigeria’s ambition to widen reliable electricity access. The programme forms part of Solad’s broader strategy of delivering decentralised energy at multiple levels; from individual homes and micro-enterprises through to market-scale mini-grids and commercial and industrial solar installations.
Solad’s Solar Home Systems programme is being implemented within the rapidly expanding ecosystem created by the Rural Electrification Agency and the World Bank-supported Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-Up (DARES) programme.
DARES represents one of Africa’s most ambitious programmes of its kind and is designed to accelerate renewable electricity access through both solar-hybrid mini-grids and standalone solar systems.
For Solad, the significance of the programme extends beyond the number of systems installed: each connection can support real economic activity. Solar electricity allows a small retailer to remain open longer, a tailor to operate electrical equipment without relying on a petrol generator, a household to power lighting and communication equipment, and a micro-enterprise to redirect money previously spent on fuel towards growing the business.
The Chief Executive of Solad’s Nigerian businesses, Yewande Olagbende, in a statement said: “Nigeria’s energy-access challenge cannot be solved by a single technology or a single type of infrastructure. We need solutions at every level; from large power infrastructure to mini-grids and individual solar systems.
“Solar Home Systems are particularly important because they can be deployed quickly and directly into communities where conventional grid expansion may take many years to arrive.
“For Solad, this is fundamentally about economic empowerment. When reliable electricity reaches a home or small business, the impact goes far beyond keeping the lights on. It creates additional working hours, reduces dependence on expensive generators, and gives entrepreneurs a more reliable foundation on which to build their businesses.”
Solad’s latest deployment builds on a long-standing involvement in Nigeria’s distributed energy sector. The Company has developed and operated energy infrastructure serving businesses and communities across Nigeria and has previously participated in programmes administered by the Rural Electrification Agency under the Nigeria Electrification Project. Solad’s portfolio today spans Solar Home Systems, mini-grids, commercial and industrial solar, battery storage, and decentralised energy infrastructure.
The company’s experience demonstrates the increasingly vital role indigenous private-sector developers can play in translating national energy-access policy and development finance into operating infrastructure on the ground.
Beyond expanding access to electricity, Solad presents its Solar Home Systems programme as a platform for local enterprise growth, job creation, and long-term customer support.
Nigeria’s renewable energy market is entering a period of significant expansion, with large-scale programmes supported by the federal government, Rural Electrification Agency, World Bank Group, and other development finance institutions combining public-sector support with private-sector execution and capital.
That combination is helping to shift the sector from individual renewable energy projects towards a more scalable distributed energy industry.
Solad said it believes that three elements will be critical to that transition: deployment at scale, strong local operating capability, and reliable long-term customer support. This is why the company’s investment extends beyond equipment.
Solad is building teams of technicians, sales and customer-support personnel capable of operating across the communities in which its systems are installed. The company recently brought together members of its DARES technical and customer-service teams for dedicated training focused on after-sales service and maintenance of deployed Solar Home Systems.
Constantine ‘Labi Ogunbiyi, the chairman and co-founder of Solad Power Group, said: “Africa’s energy transition will ultimately be judged by what gets built and by the economic activity that infrastructure enables.
“The opportunity presented by programmes such as DARES is to combine public policy, development capital and private-sector execution to build a genuinely scalable decentralised energy market.
“Solad has been working in this market for several years. Our focus now is execution; deploying more systems, expanding our operating footprint and demonstrating that African renewable energy businesses can build commercially sustainable platforms while delivering meaningful social and economic impact.”
On the Solad’s rollout, the Head of the Nigeria Electrification Programme (NEP) at the Rural Electrification Agency (REA), Femi Akinyelure, said: “The DARES programme is designed to significantly expand access to reliable and sustainable electricity by creating the conditions for distributed renewable energy solutions to be deployed at scale. A central part of this approach is enabling capable private-sector providers to extend standalone solar and mini-grid solutions to underserved households, businesses and communities across Nigeria.
“Through DARES, we are building on the experience and lessons of the Nigeria Electrification Project to move from individual interventions towards a larger, more sustainable market for distributed renewable energy. Our focus is not only on the number of connections delivered, but on ensuring that expanded electricity access supports livelihoods, productive economic activity and improved quality of life for Nigerians.”
Solar Home Systems form one component of Solad’s wider clean energy strategy. The group is developing and operating solutions across the energy spectrum, ranging from household and MSME systems to market-scale renewable energy infrastructure and commercial and industrial installations. Solad has deployed approximately 6.2 MW of clean and renewable energy capacity, and its operational footprint includes projects serving businesses and communities as well as commercial and industrial customers.
The company sees significant opportunity in connecting these different segments into a broader distributed energy platform capable of providing reliable power wherever conventional electricity supply remains inadequate. Building on its existing Solar Home System rollout, Solad intends to continue expanding that platform while investing in the people, technology and operating infrastructure required to support customers over the long term.
Olagbende added: “The next stage of Nigeria’s renewable energy story is about scale. We have demonstrated that the technology works. We now need to demonstrate that we can build the distribution, financing, technical and customer-service infrastructure required to reach millions more people. That is the opportunity Solad is positioning itself to address.”

title: California backs $18m tribal bid to buy 357 coastal acres for restoration
content:
California has approved $5 million towards the purchase of 357 coastal acres in Cayucos that once housed the largest abalone farm in the US. The yak titʸu titʸu yak tiłhini Northern Chumash Tribe is seeking to buy the property for $18 million and restore parts of the land and its former aquaculture operation.
According to The Tribune, the property, known as Alexander Ranch, has about one mile of coastline. It includes a eucalyptus grove that provides monarch butterfly habitat, a seasonal creek flowing into the Estero Bluffs and hills covered with grasses, sage and willow trees.
The tribe's nonprofit organisation entered into a purchase agreement with the estate of engineer John Alexander in 2024. The fundraising deadline is October 15, when the escrow period ends. As of June 2026, the organisation had raised almost $8.2 million, including a $7 million grant from California's Sustainable Agricultural Lands Conservation Program.
According to Becca Lucas Thomas, executive director of the ytt Northern Chumash Nonprofit, the land has a long connection with her people. Before Alexander used the property for aquaculture, it was home to an Indigenous village called tsitxala.
The tribe had harvested abalone from the coast for thousands of years.
“This property is really special. It holds a lot of history. To have the opportunity to bring this place back to our families today is really remarkable," Thomas says, as quoted by The Tribune.
Tribe plans restoration work
If the purchase goes through, the tribe plans to manage the property using indigenous stewardship practices. The proposed restoration work includes repairing habitats in the Villa Creek watershed, with the aim of supporting the return of steelhead trout.
The project is called yatspasini wa yaktspu Conservancy, meaning 'Ocean to land conservancy'. Lucas Thomas saysthe landscape had been actively managed by indigenous people before colonists forcibly removed them.
The tribe historically transplanted selected plant species, maintained waterways and used intentional burning to manage the landscape.
“While we look at this beautiful coastline, remember that it looks this way intentionally. It was created by our ancestors,” Thomas says.
The property also offers a place for the tribe to reconnect with its ancestral land. Thomas says members could eventually gather and camp there without having to seek permission from another landowner or rent a campsite.
The former abalone farm, closed in 2020, is part of the $18 million Alexander Ranch sought by the Northern Chumash Tribe.
Former abalone farm could reopen
The property also contains the remains of an abalone farm built during the 1960s. At its peak, the farm raised about 1 million abalone each year for meat.
The facility closed in 2020. About 900 concrete aquaculture tanks have remained unused since then. The Harmony Coast Aquaculture Institute currently leases the facility and wants to work with the tribe on bringing the farm back into operation.
Ben Ruttenberg, co-founder of the Harmony Coast Aquaculture Institute and director of Cal Poly's Center for Coastal Marine Sciences, said of ytt Tribe, "They are the perfect partner. This was originally their land.”
The institute also holds a state permit for the farm's seawater intake pipe. According to Ruttenberg, the pipe can bring in about 7,000 gallons of seawater per minute. He said such permits are very difficult to obtain and are important for an aquaculture operation.
The proposed system would use algae as part of the water treatment process. Seawater would first be pumped into an algae tank, where the algae would absorb nutrients. This would lower the water's carbon content and acidity before it reaches the abalone tanks.
That is important because abalone build their calcium carbonate shells more effectively in less acidic water. The farm could also use the algae as food for the abalone. The animals need large amounts of food and can take about five years to reach market size.
After passing through the abalone tanks, the water would have higher carbon content and acidity because of the animals' waste. It would therefore pass through another algae tank before being released back into the ocean.
“Our goal here is to produce excellent water that is better than the water we brought in, or at least cleaner and has less carbon dioxide than the water we pumped in,” Ruttenberg said.
Farm could support abalone restoration
The planned operation would not only focus on producing abalone for food. The tribe also hopes to use part of the facility for research and restoration.
The former farm raised red abalone. Lucas Thomas said the tribe hopes to continue raising red abalone while also working with endangered white and black abalone for restoration.
Black abalone are different from other abalone because they live in the intertidal zone. This is the part of the coast that is covered by the ocean during high tide and exposed to air during low tide. Other abalone species live in deeper water.
Tribal members recently surveying the property found black abalone along the coastline. Lucas Thomas said that could make the property a useful location for black abalone restoration work.
Scientists already understand how to raise white abalone in captivity and move them into the wild. However, there have been few successful attempts to raise black abalone on a farm.
Lucas Thomas said some of the existing aquaculture facility could be used to study how black abalone can be raised in captivity.
The project also has a cultural importance for the tribe because abalone has long been an important food source. California closed the recreational abalone fishery, while buying the molluscs has become expensive, leaving the tribe without consistent access to them.
“Many of our elders grew up with abalone being a fixture,” Lucas Thomas said. “That just hasn’t been a thing for 30, 40 years.”
Tribal members eat abalone and also use its shells to make jewellery and decorate regalia.
“To be able to have access not only back and steady, but within our control, as something that we’d be able to provide directly for our community. It’s a really, really important piece of this for us,” Lucas Thomas said.

title: A Farmer’s Son Saw His Father Struggle. Now He Helps 50,000 Farmers Earn From Solar Power
content: It is barely past dawn when Nikhil Patel reaches his field. For years, watering his crops came with a familiar worry. Would there be electricity when he needed it? Would he have to depend on the diesel pump again? This morning looks different. Rows of solar panels stand along the edge of his land. The solar-powered pump begins drawing water towards his crops. There is another change too: his farm can now earn from the sun shining over it. And Nikhil is not alone. Across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha, thousands of farmers are turning to solar power in similar ways. Behind this effort is Bhavesh Patidar, who grew up in a farming family in Khalghat, Madhya Pradesh, and closely saw how difficult it could be for a farmer to earn a stable income. He later studied at IIT and built a career in technology before founding Solarsure. Since its launch in November 2024, the company says it has commissioned over 300 MW of solar capacity and reached more than 50,000 farmers through its projects. ‘I didn’t research the problem, I lived it’ Growing up in a farming family, Bhavesh witnessed the uncertainty that defined agricultural life. His father worked tirelessly on the farm for decades, yet financial security always seemed out of reach. But there was one thing he heard his father say again and again over the years. “Pura jeevan kheti mein laga diya, par kabhi achhi kamai nahi hui.”(I spent my entire life farming, but never earned a truly good income.) The words lingered long after Bhavesh left home. Solar panels installed along the edge of Nikhil Patel’s farm now help power irrigation while creating another source of income for his family. They stayed with him as he went on to study at IIT-BHU and build a career in technology. He founded the agritech startup Neurafarms, which was later acquired, and spent years working with data-driven systems and climate-tech. But even as his work took him in a different direction, the problem he had grown up seeing at home remained familiar. “The problem was never something I discovered through research,” Bhavesh says. “I had lived it and seen it every day growing up.” Years later, the government’s PM-KUSUM scheme gave him a chance to do something about it. The scheme allows farmers to use solar in different ways, from powering irrigation pumps to setting up larger grid-connected plants and selling the electricity they generate. Bhavesh was interested in the latter: could the land itself become another source of income? He decided to test the idea on his own family’s land. Under the scheme, he set up a 2 MW solar plant and began selling electricity back to the grid. Unlike farm income, which could rise and fall with the weather and market prices, the income from solar was more predictable. Neighbouring farmers began noticing the plant and asking how it worked, and whether they could do something similar on their own land. That experiment eventually became ‘Solarsure’. Bhavesh launched the Indore-based renewable energy Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) company in November 2024. Today, it works across Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh and Odisha, helping farmers set up solar projects on underused or less-fertile land. Through solar projects, farmers can use underused or less-fertile land to generate electricity and supply it to the grid. Solarsure says over 50,000 farmers have participated in its projects, with company estimates suggesting income increases of more than 30 percent. So far, the company has commissioned over 300 MW of solar capacity and built a project pipeline exceeding 1.5 GW. What if farmers could sell power too? For many farmers, the definition of solar energy starts and ends with irrigation pumps, but Bhavesh believes the opportunity is much bigger. “Farmers should not only consume energy,” he says. “They should be able to produce and sell it as well.” Through Solarsure, farmers receive support at every stage of the process — from project design and financing assistance to installation, maintenance, and grid integration. The company develops both ground-mounted and rooftop solar systems while helping farmers access government schemes and financing options. Before a project is commissioned, Solarsure also uses AI and satellite data from agencies such as ISRO and NASA to study climate risks, wind conditions and long-term site suitability. The idea is to understand how well a site is likely to perform and optimise energy generation over time. Solarsure uses AI and satellite data to assess factors such as climate risks, wind conditions and site suitability before setting up solar projects. The company also provides the digital infrastructure needed for effective grid integration, ensuring that electricity generated by solar plants can be supplied reliably to the grid. For Bhavesh, all of this technology matters because of what it can change for a farmer’s income. “In farming, too much depends on factors outside a farmer's control,” he says. “Solar creates a second stream of income that is predictable and long-term.” ‘Now, I have a fixed monthly income’ Back in Nikhil’s field, you can see the transformation beautifully play out. A farmer by occupation, Nikhil first came across information about solar projects under the PM-KUSUM scheme through social media. Curious, he began researching the concept and eventually connected with Solarsure. At the time, financial pressures were mounting. “There was a money crisis,” he recalls. “I wanted to understand whether this could really work.” After learning more about the process, he decided to move forward. Looking back, he calls it one of the best decisions of his life. “Earlier, I faced many problems financially,” he says. “Now I receive a fixed income every month. My EMIs are managed, and I can plan for the future.” The additional income has also given him confidence to explore other opportunities. “Today I can make decisions easily. Whether it is for my family or a small side business, I have the confidence to move ahead.” For Nikhil, the solar project has brought a fixed monthly income, helping him manage EMIs and plan ahead for his family. For Nikhil, being able to plan ahead is perhaps the biggest change. And after seeing what solar has done for his own finances, he wants other farmers to at least understand the option available to them. “The weather is uncertain, and farming incomes are not fixed. If farmers want better earnings and a better life, they should understand solar power and explore the PM-KUSUM scheme.” While Nikhil points to a fixed monthly earning, another farmer, Mitesh, has experienced the financial benefit in a different way: through lower household electricity costs. Living in a 20-member joint family, he once paid electricity bills of around Rs 12,000 every month. After installing a 5-kW solar system, that figure dropped dramatically. “Today my electricity bill is only around Rs 1,000 to Rs 1,200. I save nearly Rs 10,000 to Rs 12,000 every month.” From paying EMIs to planning ahead For a farmer, an extra source of income can change very ordinary decisions. An EMI gets paid on time. An electricity bill no longer eats into the month’s earnings. There is a little more room to think about the next crop, a child’s education, or an expense at home without wondering where the money will come from. That is what makes solar interesting to Bhavesh. Farming will still depend on rain, crop prices and a hundred things a farmer cannot control. But the sunlight falling on the same piece of land can give the family something else to rely on. Sometimes that means cheaper electricity. Sometimes it means water for the field. And sometimes, as Nikhil found, it means knowing that some money will come in even when the farming season does not go as planned. From lower electricity bills to additional income, solar power is helping farming families find another way to make their land and resources work for them. This takes Bhavesh back to something he heard from his father for years: that a lifetime of farming had still not brought the financial security he had hoped for. Today, Bhavesh hopes he can help other farming families write a different story, one where the land beneath their feet and the sun above their heads can both help them build a more secure future. “If farmers can earn with dignity and build financial security for their families, then we've achieved something meaningful,” he smiles. title: Onderzoeksrapport Handelingsperspectief dankzij burgerwetenschap
content:
Wat burgerwetenschap allemaal teweegbrengt is niet altijd direct zichtbaar. Waag Futurelab onderzocht de mogelijkheden die burgerwetenschap biedt voor bewoners, overheden en kennisinstellingen. De publicatie Handelingsperspectief dankzij burgerwetenschap deelt de belangrijkste bevindingen van het onderzoek.
Burgerwetenschap is in opkomst. In heel Nederland zijn er gemeenschappen actief die metingen doen van de luchtkwaliteit, waterkwaliteit, biodiversiteit, geluid, bodem en allerlei andere aspecten van de leefomgeving. Steeds meer (lokale) overheden en kennisinstellingen werken samen met bewoners aan dit soort onderzoeken en maatschappelijke vraagstukken.
Burgerwetenschap levert niet alleen meer kennis op, maar brengt ook andere acties op gang. Toch is het niet altijd zichtbaar voor betrokkenen wat burgerwetenschap allemaal teweegbrengt. Waag Futurelab onderzocht de handelingsperspectieven (mogelijke acties) die burgerwetenschap biedt voor bewoners, overheden en kennisinstellingen. De publicatie 'Handelingsperspectief dankzij burgerwetenschap' deelt de belangrijkste bevindingen van het onderzoek. Daarbij beschrijft het de waarde van burgerwetenschap, de uitdagingen, en welke stappen er nodig zijn om van inzicht tot verandering te komen.
Op basis van de inzichten van het onderzoek naar handelingsperspectieven is het samenwerkingsspel Aan Zet! ontwikkeld. Aan Zet! helpt om spelenderwijs inzichtelijk te maken welke handelingsperspectieven burgerwetenschap biedt. Het spel is zowel voor gemeenschappen, (lokale) overheden als kennisinstellingen goed toepasbaar om samen in gesprek te gaan over burgerwetenschapsprojecten en een plan op te stellen om daar samen aan te werken.
Wil je meer weten over Aan Zet! of wil je het spel graag spelen? Neem contact met ons op via support [at] hollandse-luchten [dot] org.
Totstandkoming
Het onderzoek naar handelingsperspectieven komt voort uit het burgerwetenschapsproject Hollandse Luchten. Er zijn inzichten uit de meetgroepen van Hollandse Luchten gedocumenteerd en verschillende mensen geïnterviewd. Daarnaast zijn er ook een aantal voorbeelden toegevoegd vanuit andere burgerwetenschapsprojecten. Deze publicatie is in eerste instantie gericht op burgermeetprojecten waarbinnen luchtkwaliteit gemeten wordt met burgerwetenschapssensoren, maar zijn ook breed toepasbaar voor andere burgerwetenschapsprojecten waarin gemeenschappen, (lokale) overheden en kennisinstellingen samenwerken.

title: Faith-Aligned Finance Is the Original Trust Capital (Blog)
content:
The social sector has spent the last five years congratulating itself for discovering trust. Championing unrestricted grants, multi-year commitments, and deference to community judgment, trust-based philanthropy is now the field’s favorite innovation, complete with conferences, pledges, and a growing literature on why funders should stop treating grantees like suspects. Only two months ago, someone stopped me mid-sentence when I said “grantees” and asked me to use “partners” instead to honor this new trust and power dynamic.
The discovery is roughly 14 centuries late. In some traditions, longer.
Faith-aligned finance—including zakat, waqf, tithe, tzedakah, dasond, and other religious giving traditions—has operated as codified trust capital for centuries. These systems operate with a consistency, scale and nuance most institutional funders struggle to fathom, through mechanisms that took on the sector’s hardest problems long before the sector existed.
Development finance largely treats faith-aligned finance as a niche pool of capital to tap or faith institutions as delivery partners to enlist. However, the arrangements through which religious traditions govern giving, establish legitimacy, and hold stewards accountable are of greater value. These already exist within traditions. The unfinished work is connecting them with public and philanthropic financing without stripping away the obligations that make them meaningful. Development finance should study their design, not simply fundraise from it.
How I Learned This
I came to this through failure. In 2011, the Libyan revolution broke out. I was a final-year medical student in Zawia and founded Voice of Libyan Women, an organization that campaigned for inclusive security leadership and women’s agency. The team’s early work led with the language of international advocacy: rights, conventions, statistics. Embassies thought we were darling, but both they and the people who attended our events were already persuaded of our cause. For most families, the message was accurate, but it felt unauthorized; they heard it as something that arrived from outside the community’s moral framing.
So we rebuilt and reframed, working directly with Libya’s Dar al-Ifta, the national institution responsible for religious rulings, to formally endorse the Quranic verses and hadiths (sayings and traditions of the Prophet Muhammad) that supported women’s agency and leadership. The endorsement took more than a year—we showed up at their offices whenever they would see us and answered their questions on their terms and on their timeline—but it changed the source of authority behind the argument for women’s agency; what the community originally heard as an imported rights claim now carried religious legitimacy. It also opened doors to local funding. We then launched the Noor Campaign (noor means “light” in Arabic) as a public initiative of Voice of Libyan Women.
People in the oasis city of Sabha and people in the coastal city of Zawia hear each other very differently, so we also built city teams led by teachers, doctors, faith leaders, mothers, and young people whom local communities already trusted. Many told us that they had agreed with the organization’s position from the beginning but engaged only after we made it more socially acceptable for them to participate publicly.
Funders usually agree on the need. What they lack are structures capable of satisfying fiduciary and religious obligations at the same time.
Development practice often assumes that the binding constraint is supply, yet many well-designed interventions fail at implementation—vaccines expire in warehouses, books sit unopened. Despite cold-chain investment, intensive surveillance, and political negotiation, for example, Northern Nigeria’s polio resurgence in the early 2000s didn’t resolve until religious and traditional leaders helped rebuild public confidence, allowing immunization campaigns to resume. Similarly, the Noor Campaign meant that the same argument that had stalled for months traveled across the country—appearing in Friday sermons and on national television during Ramadan—in weeks. I came to think of “permission” as the collective social authorization that determines whether people feel they can act on an option that technically exists. I later called the distance between what communities materially need and what they feel morally or socially sanctioned to accept the “permission gap.”
I have watched the permission gap operate from every side of the table since. Leading a conflict-prevention firm, I saw its inverse. Where legitimate institutions vacate the permission space, violent actors can move into it, financing themselves through distorted claims on the very same sacred obligations. Trust is not inherently virtuous; the same combination of moral authority, networks, and capital can legitimize exclusion as readily as access. Transnational “family values” campaigns, funded by religious networks in the United States and Netherlands, demonstrate this across parts of Africa. The case for engaging faith-aligned finance rests on its influence, not its moral exceptionalism: Faith shapes who gives, whose judgment carries weight, and what communities consider legitimate. Those are forms of power that any serious account of development finance has to take seriously.
Years later, directing global advocacy and policy at one of the world’s largest foundations, I watched the gap manifest at institutional scale. Immaculately designed technical programs underperformed wherever uptake required that people act against the principles they understood their faith or community sanctioned. What startled me wasn’t the pattern; Libya had taught me that a decade earlier. It was the altitude at which it survived. Permission was often absent from program design because the tools organizations used to plan programs did not see it.
The Original Trust Architecture
Faith-aligned finance can help close the permission gap by embedding religious legitimacy in the financing itself. Consider zakat, a Quranic obligation requiring that Muslims transfer 2.5 percent of qualifying wealth each year. The Quran specifies eight categories of eligible recipients, including the poor, the indebted, and those in bondage, creating an eligibility standard set at origin and resistant to donor or institutional drift. The obligation is enforced primarily by conscience rather than a revenue authority, and conscience is a remarkably effective collector: Humanitarian financing analyses describe zakat as one of the largest sources of humanitarian funding in the world. Estimates of total annual giving range from $200 billion to $1 trillion. Even the lower estimate exceeds all tracked global humanitarian assistance several times over.
Waqf, its endowment counterpart, solves for perpetuity by permanently dedicating an asset to a charitable purpose. As governments rise and fall, its principal cannot be sold, seized, or repurposed. For example, Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, founded by Fatima al-Fihri in 859 and sustained through waqf, remains among the world's oldest continuously operating universities. Accountability has a religious dimension: A zakat payer understands the transfer as a religious obligation, and the intermediary holds a responsibility that is both fiduciary and sacred.
Taken together, these mechanisms address problems conventional philanthropy repeatedly struggles with, including who is eligible, what the money may be used for, how long the obligation lasts, and who the steward is accountable to. They also attach legitimacy to the capital before it arrives.
I call this potential advantage the “permission premium.” It can operate at two points: when a giver recognizes a financing structure as a legitimate way to fulfill an obligation, and when a community recognizes that the services it supports are legitimate to use. Evidence of the first does not, by itself, establish the second.
The Permission Premium in Practice
The Noor Campaign left me with a recurring question: What if philanthropy treated faith institutions not merely as messengers or implementers, but as part of the infrastructure determining what communities trust, finance, and use?
In 2022, I began pitching a financing vehicle built on that premise, and after more than a year of building a strategy, financing model, and coalition, I created For Mama, the first zakat-eligible, Muslim-led funder collaborative for maternal and newborn health. The collaborative made maternal and newborn health legible within zakat giving, and raised $13 million in our first Ramadan campaign. Across three Ramadan campaigns, For Mama, now known as Every Pregnancy, has raised $125 million from more than 190,000 individual donors, including many outside traditional global health financing.
The multilateral system has also built structures that make participation religiously legitimate for donors, if unevenly. UNHCR’s Refugee Zakat Fund, which launched in 2017, has dedicated rules for collecting and distributing zakat. Islamic legal opinions known as fatwas, support these, giving donors a way to fulfill a religious obligation through a compliant structure.
Capital markets offer another example. When the International Finance Facility for Immunization, which raises capital-market financing for Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, issued its first vaccine sukuk (an investment certificate that’s compliant with the body of religious law called Sharia and is often compared with a bond) in 2014, it raised $500 million—the largest debut sukuk of its kind. A second issuance raised $200 million the following year—roughly three-quarters of a billion dollars, mobilized through an instrument the development establishment still files under “niche.”
The evidence isn’t universal, but where faith-aligned instruments are governed credibly, they repeatedly mobilize capital by embedding religious legitimacy, donor intent, and accountability into the instrument itself. The pattern extends far beyond Islam. The Franciscan monti di pietà of 15th-century Italy are described as precursors to modern microcredit. The Jewish tradition of interest-free lending inspired the Hebrew Free Loan Societies, and New York's has operated since 1892. The Buddhist Tzu Chi Foundation began in 1966 with 30 Taiwanese housewives saving coins in bamboo banks and grew into a major global humanitarian organization. Even modern environmental, social, and governance investing partly descends from faith-aligned financing, including Methodist and Quaker investment screens. Across traditions, the architecture differs, but the design principle—that shared moral commitments shape how institutions raise, govern, and sustain capital—recurs.
The Missing Infrastructure
In my work on financing maternal health, child flourishing, displacement, climate, and humanitarian response, I find that prospective funders usually agree on the need. What they lack are structures capable of satisfying fiduciary and religious obligations at the same time. In commercial Islamic finance, bodies such as the Accounting and Auditing Organization for Islamic Financial Institutions and the Islamic Financial Services Board have developed standards that help institutions assess financial products and governance across markets. For faith-aligned social finance, the practical challenge remains: How can institutions operating under different religious and fiduciary rules finance the same project?
Building blocks exist. UNHCR, for example, has built dedicated accounts, eligibility rules, compliance review, and religious guidance for its Refugee Zakat Fund. But it doesn't provide a framework for co-financing. If a government, a local zakat institution, a waqf trustee, a philanthropist, and a development finance institution all want to finance the same maternal health facility, they may have no common basis for determining which costs are zakat-eligible, how a waqf can endow or hold the asset, or what evidence will satisfy a Sharia board, foundation trustees, and an investment committee. Getting them into a single structure today would require months of bespoke legal, scholarly, and financial work that most deals do not survive.
This helps explain an apparent paradox. Hundreds of billions may move through zakat each year, yet formal zakat institutions are estimated to capture only $10 billion to $15 billion of total zakat giving. Read carelessly, this looks like inefficiency awaiting formalization. But it is the thesis in miniature: Givers need confidence that their money reaches eligible recipients and is distributed according to the rules of the obligation. Some gain that confidence by giving directly to people they know; others rely on a local institution or a larger fund with credible religious oversight and clear reporting.
The task for development finance is to design accordingly and meet those requirements, not assume that institutional scale itself earns trust. What is missing is the connective tissue.
What To Do About It
Before a foundation or government commits money to a program, it decides whom the program will serve, how people will access it, which organizations will deliver it, and how they will measure success. This is the moment when it should also ask: Whose trust does this program need to earn before people will use it, and have those people helped shape how it is financed and delivered? Too often, faith leaders enter a program after its design is fixed, asked to endorse a vaccination drive or announce a clinic they had no hand in shaping. By then their role is persuasion, with little room to change the decisions that may have made the program unacceptable in the first place.
Asking early may reveal barriers that a communications campaign cannot solve after a clinic has opened or a program has launched. UNICEF’s Faith for Positive Change initiative, which builds influence mapping, faith engagement, co-design, and measurement into program design offers one approach to involving faith communities in program planning and implementation.
Beyond individual programs, the field faces the larger question of how different financing systems can work together. Here, climate finance offers a useful precedent. Green Bond Principles gave issuers and investors a common framework for identifying eligible projects and reporting how funds were used. Indonesia’s sovereign green sukuk shows what this can look like in practice: a Sharia-compliant instrument built against a green-finance framework legible to conventional, Islamic, and sustainability investors alike.
Faith-aligned and conventional institutions can build the missing architecture: agreed processes for determining zakat eligibility, waqf-compatible legal templates for development assets, and measurement frameworks that allow Sharia boards and investment committees to assess the same opportunity. Governments should meanwhile identify public priorities that these structures could finance, clarify how waqf assets and public funds can legally sit alongside other capital, and set clear rules for oversight. Larger funders should bring real projects and say what would make them willing to co-finance them, and philanthropists can provide catalytic capital to test the structures.
A practical starting point is to agree which costs each source of funding can cover. For a child-health program, that could mean establishing which services for eligible children zakat may finance, subject to the relevant religious approval, and which remaining costs government or philanthropic funding would meet. Each contributor could then support a shared objective while retaining its own obligations and accounting.
At the same time, researchers should test the permission premium rather than assume it exists. On the financing side, the question is whether these structures attract additional giving, redirect existing giving, or sustain support over longer periods. On the service side, researchers should compare otherwise similar programs and examine whether people know how they are financed, whether that knowledge affects their trust, and whether it influences their use of services. Those comparisons must account for differences in quality, cost, access, and community engagement. Researchers should also examine whether these structures sustain funding over time. I’m currently building toward that evidence through a multifaith compact and an interfaith financing facility that put these principles into practice for children’s survival and flourishing.
The scale these shared structures could unlock matters. If even 1 percent of the most conservative zakat estimate flowed through them, it would mean $2 billion a year for children—capital that can grow precisely because it is native to the contexts where permission binds hardest. The larger opportunity is to enable faith institutions, governments, and philanthropies to finance shared public priorities repeatedly, without rebuilding the legal and financial arrangements for every project. The real value should be judged by what they make possible for the people they serve.
From building the Noor Campaign in Libya to creating For Mama, I’ve seen what changes when people recognize the values and obligations built into an initiative. Too often, development finance asks communities to trust structures designed without them. The sector’s trust deficit is partly the legacy of financing structures that still presume communities must prove themselves to distant funders. Faith traditions have spent centuries building ways to give, govern, and account for money through shared commitments, and that architecture deserves to shape what we build next.
