title: Medellin Native David Velez to Invest US$1.58B in Colombia, Calls for End to Usury Cap
content:
David Velez, the Medellin-born founder and CEO of Nubank, plans to invest approximately US$1.58 billion in Colombia between 2026 and 2030 as the digital bank expands its presence in the country.
Velez announced the investment alongside Nu Colombia General Manager Marcela Torres and Colombia Fintech President Gabriel Santos, saying the company intends to remain in Colombia for the long term.
Nu entered Colombia in 2021 with a credit card and has since expanded its financial products. The company now holds more than US$3.49 billion in deposits across savings accounts and CDTs, or fixed-term deposit certificates.
Velez said Nu grew from zero to five million customers within five years, including customers who previously lacked access to credit, and that the company’s next goal is to become one of Colombia’s leading financial institutions.
The planned US$1.58 billion investment will focus on four areas: advanced data and artificial intelligence platforms, new financial services, expansion of strategic teams, and capital to support what Velez described as “responsible, scaled growth.”
How David Velez plans to expand Nubank in Colombia
Torres also presented figures on Nu’s position in Colombia’s banking sector, saying the company now has the fourth-largest base of individual deposits nationwide.
Nu currently holds roughly 10% of Colombia’s credit card market and about 7% of individual deposits, according to figures presented by the company. It has reached 6 million customers, equivalent to approximately 14% to 15% of Colombia’s adult population.
Torres said Nu’s credit card business is growing 60% year over year. She also argued that without the company’s growth, Colombia’s overall credit card market would have contracted.
According to Nu, nearly 40% of customers who joined the company over the past year had no previous relationship with Colombia’s financial sector.
The company also said it accounted for 25% of people who gained access to credit nationwide during the same period, despite holding about 10% of the credit card market.
Women represented 59% of those newly included customers, compared with what Nu described as a sector average of 41%.
Torres acknowledged that credit risk could increase as the company expands lending to populations that have historically had less access to the formal financial system.
Why David Velez wants to end Colombia’s usury cap
Velez also called for changes to Colombia’s usury rate, the maximum interest rate lenders are legally permitted to charge.
He described the cap as “the biggest obstacle to financial inclusion in Colombia,” arguing that it limits regulated financial institutions’ ability to lend to higher-risk customers.
According to Velez, only 20% of Colombia’s population has access to credit, leaving many others dependent on informal lenders, including those known as “gota a gota,” or daily-payment lenders.
He said interest rates charged by such lenders can range from 500% to 2,000%, while borrowers do not receive the consumer protections available through regulated financial institutions.
Velez argued that because regulated banks cannot price loans according to the risk associated with individual borrowers beyond the legal ceiling, lenders may reject higher-risk applicants rather than extend credit.
He proposed two possible changes. The first would end the practice of combining different credit products when calculating a single usury ceiling and instead establish separate limits for different types of credit.
The second would eliminate the interest rate cap altogether, a measure Velez argues would increase credit availability for consumers and small businesses.
Velez said he hopes Colombia’s next administration will address the issue, arguing that changes involving interest rates, reduced dependence on cash and faster implementation of open finance regulations could significantly accelerate financial inclusion.

title: Meta Expands Teen Safety With New Parental Supervision Features In India
content:
Meta has begun rolling out parental supervision on Threads across the Asia-Pacific region, including India, giving parents and guardians greater visibility and control over teenagers’ use of the platform.
The tools, available through Meta’s Family Centre, allow parents to view a teenager’s Threads usage for the previous seven days, set daily time limits, restrict access during specific hours, adjust night-time settings, manage tagging and oversee certain privacy and sensitive-content preferences.
The rollout, announced by Meta in September, builds on the platform’s existing Teen Accounts, which provide protections such as private-by-default accounts and restrictions on the content teens can see.
The move comes amid growing scrutiny of Meta in India over online child safety and the circulation of child sexual abuse material (CSAM). In July, the government said it had taken serious note of reports alleging advertisements linked to CSAM on social media and sought a detailed report from the concerned intermediary, while the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) also issued notices.
The NCPCR subsequently began a formal inquiry into alleged lapses in Meta India’s child-safety policies and summoned Meta India executives. In September, Meta agreed to report child-safety cases directly to India’s cybercrime authorities through the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), rather than relying solely on the previous reporting route through the US-based National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC).
Meta said, “protecting children on our platforms is a priority” and that it was committed to working with the government to ensure perpetrators are held responsible.
More Control For Parents
Under the new Threads supervision system, parents can view how much time their teenager has spent on the platform each day over the previous week, along with the average daily usage. They can set a daily limit and block Threads during selected days or hours. If a teenager accesses Threads on multiple devices, the time limit applies to their total usage rather than separately on each device.
Parents can also adjust Threads’ sleep mode, including limiting or blocking access at night. Meta says notifications are muted and auto-replies are enabled by default between 10 pm and 7 am under sleep mode. Parents can additionally control who can tag their teenager and manage or approve certain privacy settings and sensitive-content preferences.
The controls are being introduced alongside Threads’ existing Teen Accounts. Meta says parents can decide whether teenagers under 16 can make some of the platform’s default protections less restrictive. The company has described the supervision tools as an extension of safeguards already built into Teen Accounts, rather than a replacement for its existing moderation systems.
Scrutiny Over Child Safety
The India rollout comes against the backdrop of a wider dispute over how social-media platforms detect, remove and report material involving child sexual exploitation. In July, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology said the government had taken serious note of reports concerning advertisements allegedly linked to CSAM on social-media platforms and sought detailed information from the concerned intermediary. The PIB statement also noted that NCPCR had issued notices to the platforms involved.
The NCPCR later instituted a formal inquiry into alleged shortcomings in Meta India’s child-safety policies and its handling of CSAM-related material. Meta India Managing Director Arun Srinivas was summoned by the child-rights body as part of the proceedings. Reports said the inquiry followed concerns over Meta’s response to the allegations.
The issue subsequently led to a change in Meta’s reporting arrangement in India. Business Standard reported that Meta agreed to share child sexual abuse cases and details of repeat offenders directly with Indian law-enforcement agencies through the I4C cybercrime division. Government officials said such information could include account details such as names, associated email IDs and IP addresses, which they argued could assist investigations.
The government has also indicated that it expects greater accountability from major platforms. Government sources cited by Business Standard said Meta could not be viewed simply as an intermediary because its algorithms influence what content is amplified and made visible to users.
The Logical Indian’s Perspective
Children’s safety online cannot rest on one setting, one app or one technology. Meta’s parental supervision tools can give families greater visibility and help parents establish healthier boundaries around screen time, privacy and online interactions. At the same time, parental controls should complement — not substitute — the responsibility of platforms to detect harmful material, act swiftly on reports and cooperate transparently with authorities.
The recent scrutiny in India also highlights why child safety requires cooperation between parents, technology companies, regulators, child-rights bodies and law-enforcement agencies. Parents need practical tools, teenagers need age-appropriate protection and platforms need systems that respond effectively when those safeguards fail.

title: Youth-Led Forest Restoration Movement Traces Back to a 9-Year-Old’s Question About Climate Change
content:
A boy who learned about Wangari Maathai’s tree-planting legacy at age nine sparked a youth-led forest restoration movement now training over 100,000 young Climate Justice Ambassadors across 76 countries.
Youth-led forest restoration at Plant-for-the-Planet began in 2007, when nine-year-old Felix Finkbeiner in Germany learned about Kenyan Nobel laureate Wangari Maathai’s campaign planting 30 million trees across Africa. Struck by her message that trees serve as powerful allies against global warming, Finkbeiner proposed that every country commit to planting one million trees. By age 13, he stood before the United Nations General Assembly, raising that ambition to one trillion trees worldwide.
Nearly two decades later, youth-led forest restoration has grown from one child’s conviction into a global movement operating academies across 76 countries. More than 104,800 children and youth have become Climate Justice Ambassadors, trained to understand the climate crisis and empowered to fight for their future through tree planting, public speaking, and community organizing. The organization has facilitated more than 36 million trees planted directly through its own restoration projects, while its platform has funded over 107 million trees through partner organizations worldwide.
The model driving youth-led forest restoration rests on a simple premise: young people affected most by climate change deserve genuine agency in addressing it, not token participation. At Plant-for-the-Planet Academies, Ambassadors learn climate science, then apply that knowledge locally, giving speeches, organizing tree-planting events, and mobilizing their communities. This youth leadership extends into formal governance through the Global Ambassadors Council, the organization’s official youth leadership body shaping strategic direction.
Restoration work spans three countries, each addressing distinct ecological challenges. In Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula, youth-led forest restoration protects and regrows Mayan rainforest, with more than 17.8 million trees planted, two reserves under active patrol, and work underway establishing a jaguar wildlife corridor connecting fragmented habitat. In Ghana, community-based restoration addresses degradation across the Savannah Ecological Zone, tackling climate vulnerability and poverty simultaneously through Plant-for-Ghana. In Spain, restoration projects are reviving lost forest landscapes around Granada, Doñana, Madrid, and Barcelona.
Beyond planting trees directly, youth-led forest restoration extends its impact through free technology supporting restoration organizations worldwide. Forest Cloud provides funding, management, and monitoring tools for restoration projects at no cost to nonprofits and communities, and has already enabled more than 100 million trees to be funded through the platform. FireAlert monitors 1.6 billion hectares for wildfire risk, allowing rapid response before fires spread. TreeMapper helps organizations track restoration progress with scientific rigor, while SeedManager, still in development, will support biodiverse ecosystem restoration specifically.
This technology-sharing approach reflects a deliberate strategic shift. Rather than measuring success purely by trees planted, satellite imagery and hectare-based tracking now anchor the organization’s accountability, providing longer-term verification of genuine forest recovery rather than short-term planting counts alone. Free restoration advice and published research further extend support to restoration organizations beyond Plant-for-the-Planet’s own direct projects.
Youth-led forest restoration also encompasses direct policy advocacy. The organization pushes for policies enabling forest conservation and climate justice, including transparency initiatives like TFFF Watch, which monitors accountability within international rainforest funding mechanisms, and Tracer, a tool supporting deforestation-free supply chains under European Union regulations.
National entities extend this youth-led forest restoration model across eight countries with independent operations. Ghana’s affiliate has empowered 2,400 Climate Justice Ambassadors while planting over 227,000 trees. Spain’s chapter, active since 2013, has trained over 5,100 Ambassadors through 151 academies while planting more than 501,000 trees. Since 2015, Czechia has mobilized youth and national celebrities alike, engaging over 1,000 Ambassadors. Each national entity adapts the core model, youth empowerment paired with forest restoration, to its own climate and community context.
Corporate partnerships increasingly fund this expansion. Companies can grow dedicated forest plots, support deforestation-free supply chains, and educate their workforce on climate action through structured partnership programs. Change Chocolate, a fair-trade product line, generates revenue that directly supports community forest protection in tropical regions vulnerable to deforestation pressure.
What distinguishes youth-led forest restoration from conventional reforestation charities is this persistent emphasis on intergenerational leadership. Ambassadors don’t simply volunteer for adult-designed programs; they shape strategy through elected councils, speak at international forums, and carry restoration knowledge into their own communities as they grow into adulthood. Finkbeiner himself, once a nine-year-old inspired by a Nobel laureate’s tree-planting campaign, now leads an organization where the next generation of nine-year-olds continues that same cycle of learning and action.
Nearly twenty years after one child’s question about climate change reached a global stage, youth-led forest restoration demonstrates that meaningful climate action doesn’t require waiting for adulthood or institutional permission. It requires forests, young people willing to fight for them, and the tools to turn that determination into hectares of restored, thriving ecosystems.

title: Ethiopia’s Fields Are Becoming a Laboratory for Africa’s Next Agricultural Revolution
content:
Ethiopia’s Fields Are Becoming a Laboratory for Africa’s Next Agricultural Revolution
Addis Ababa, September 21, 2026 (FMC) — Some agricultural transformations are measured in harvests. Others are measured in the number of assumptions they force an entire sector to reconsider.
Across Ethiopia, an increasingly important experiment has been unfolding not inside a single research station or demonstration plot, but across millions of hectares: what happens when improved varieties, irrigation, mechanization, cluster farming, extension systems, climate information and new production practices are taken from the laboratory and pushed toward national scale?
The answer is beginning to reshape the country’s agricultural trajectory—and to attract attention well beyond its borders.
The transformation is particularly visible in wheat. Ethiopia’s rapid expansion of irrigated wheat production brought together several elements that are often treated separately in agricultural development: heat-tolerant varieties, irrigation, improved agronomic practices, organized production, research, extension and market linkages. By 2023, heat-tolerant irrigated wheat production had reached about one million hectares, with average productivity of around four tonnes per hectare, according to research documented through the FAO agricultural knowledge platform. The approach was identified as having potential relevance for wider African food-security efforts.
That is what makes the Ethiopian experience more consequential than a single crop story.
The country has increasingly been using agriculture as a field for systems integration—bringing technologies, institutions and production models together and testing what happens when they operate at scale.
Cluster farming is one such experiment. Rather than leaving millions of smallholders to confront modern agricultural markets and technologies individually, production is increasingly organized around coordinated areas and common production practices. Ethiopia says its cluster-farming system now involves about 9.5 million farmers cultivating 12.8 million hectares, with reported gains in productivity and farmer incomes.
Irrigation represents another major shift.
For generations, much of Ethiopian agriculture has been tied closely to the rhythm of seasonal rainfall. Expanding irrigation changes that equation by allowing farmers to manage water rather than simply wait for it. It can create additional production seasons, diversify crops and reduce exposure to erratic rainfall. The World Bank has identified irrigation as a central pathway for increasing agricultural productivity and strengthening food security in Ethiopia, including through multiple cropping seasons and greater production of diverse and drought-resistant crops.
The significance is not simply that more land is being irrigated.
It is that the production calendar itself can be redesigned.
The same logic extends to seeds. Improved varieties adapted to different agro-ecological conditions—including heat-tolerant wheat—are allowing production systems to move into environments once considered considerably more difficult. Research on Ethiopia’s irrigated wheat expansion has highlighted the role of improved varieties, cluster farming, research institutions, extension services and private-sector actors in bringing these technologies together at scale.
Mechanization adds another layer.
Agricultural modernization cannot be reduced to putting tractors into fields. It involves changing the economics and timing of land preparation, planting, harvesting, threshing, transport and post-harvest handling. Ethiopia’s agricultural development priorities explicitly include expanding mechanization alongside irrigation, horticulture, private-sector participation and institutional capacity.
And increasingly, the experiment is becoming digital.
Weather and climate information, for example, can become a production input in its own right. Research involving Ethiopian farming households found that access to weather and climate services was associated with productivity increases of 27 percent for maize and 17 percent for wheat, underscoring the potential value of information alongside physical inputs such as fertilizer and improved seed.
Taken together, these developments point toward a different understanding of agricultural innovation.
The important question is no longer only whether Ethiopia can produce a better seed, introduce a new machine, expand irrigation or teach a better farming technique. The larger question is whether these components can be assembled into a functioning production system and reproduced at national scale.
That is where Ethiopia’s agricultural experience becomes potentially continental in significance.
Africa does not lack agricultural potential. It has land, water, diverse agro-ecologies, a vast farming population and enormous domestic and regional markets. What has often been missing is the capacity to convert those assets consistently into productivity, reliable supply, commercial value and food-system resilience.
Ethiopia’s ongoing experiment is therefore less about discovering one magical agricultural solution than about testing how several solutions can work together.
Its emerging model is built around a simple but powerful proposition: productivity can be engineered.
Water can be managed. Production seasons can be extended. Varieties can be adapted. Farms can be organized. Information can reach farmers. Machinery can reduce bottlenecks. Research can feed directly into production. Markets can pull output through the value chain.
None of these changes eliminates the country’s agricultural challenges. Ethiopia still faces droughts, floods, pests, conflict-related disruptions, market constraints and serious food-security problems in vulnerable areas. FAO continues to report significant food-security pressures, particularly in pastoral regions affected by climatic and economic shocks.
But precisely because the challenges remain, the scale of the agricultural experiment matters.
Ethiopia is testing whether a predominantly smallholder agricultural economy can progressively move from vulnerability toward greater productivity, diversification and resilience without waiting for every constraint to disappear first.
That makes the Ethiopian countryside something more than the traditional backdrop to a national development story.
It is becoming a living testing ground for African agricultural transformation.
The most consequential harvest may therefore not be measured only in tonnes of wheat, maize, coffee or other crops. It may be measured in knowledge: which technologies work in which environments, which production systems can scale, which institutional arrangements improve farmer productivity, and which combinations can turn Africa’s enormous agricultural potential into dependable food and economic capacity.
If those lessons can travel—from Ethiopia’s irrigated lowlands to other African production zones, from research institutions to farmers, and from individual crops to entire food systems—the experiment taking place in Ethiopian fields could ultimately become part of something much larger.
Not simply an agricultural transformation in one country.
A laboratory for the continent.

title: Mid-Autumn traditions come alive at Ho Chi Minh City art exhibition
content:
The gallery is divided into three spaces inspired by traditional Vietnamese architecture.
At the center is the independent installation Thung Thinh Thung, featuring four northern Vietnamese folk-style lion heads from the Trang Ta traditional toy restoration project suspended above traditional drums.
The lion heads are handcrafted from bamboo and rattan frames, papier-mâché, fabric, and rustic decorative motifs.
Visitors can also listen to a contemporary folk instrumental work composed specifically for the exhibition by artist Dzung.
Other spaces display gouache paintings and works on do paper by renowned painter Nguyen Tu Nghiem, featuring zodiac animals and festivals, alongside a collection of Mid-Autumn-themed woodblock prints.
Through familiar images of lion dances, lantern processions, and full-moon nights, artists from different generations offer new interpretations of folk memories.
Kevin Vuong, the artist behind the Trang Ta project, said his interest in lion dancing began in childhood and later inspired him to recreate the traditional lion.
He said the broader aim is to bring this cultural tradition into everyday life instead of leaving it only in museums or allowing it to be forgotten.
Through the exhibition, Vuong hopes to encourage greater appreciation of Vietnamese folk art.
Tho, co-founder of EMGallery, said the gallery chose the Mid-Autumn Festival theme to create a timely exhibition while helping spread traditional culture more widely in the community.
The exhibition also features an art talk, Folk Art: The Road to Modernity, at 2:30 pm on Saturday, with Kevin Vuong, collector Thanh Uy, contemporary instrumental artist Dzung, and Tho.
A workshop on decorating traditional northern Vietnamese lion heads will take place on Sunday, with sessions from 9:30 am to noon and from 2:30 pm to 5:00 pm. Participants will also hear the Trang Ta team share the story behind the traditional lion-head design.

title: Sign language access key to protect children with disability: Minister
content:
"Sign language enables individuals to build relationships, access information, learn, express themselves, voice opinions, make decisions on their own lives, and participate in social life. For deaf children, access to communication is not merely a technical issue but a fundamental part of fulfilling children's rights," she said in a statement on Thursday.
The minister made the statement during the 2026 International Day of Sign Languages Campaign.
Arifah noted that limited communication access can affect many areas of children's lives, from education and access to information to social interaction and self-expression.
Adequate communication access enables children to communicate when they feel scared, uncomfortable, or sick, and to speak up about bullying or violence, she added.
To this end, the ministry continues to advocate for equal access to women and child protection services, including through the SAPA 129 hotline for women and children with disabilities.
"We must ensure that every victim who wants to speak out has the means to report their experience. We must prevent children who experience violence from being unable to explain what happened simply because those around them cannot communicate with them," Arifah stated.
Therefore, disability-friendly services should not be viewed as mere add-ons. Instead, inclusivity must be an integral part of the service quality itself, she continued.
Meanwhile, Iwan Satriyawan Setyohadi, an Indonesian Sign Language instructor from the Indonesian Sign Language Center in Jakarta, explained that Indonesian Sign Language (Bisindo) is the natural language of the deaf community. It possesses distinct linguistic characteristics and is not universal.
Understanding deaf language and culture is crucial to establishing inclusive communication, he noted.
"By learning sign language, we not only gain the ability to communicate with deaf individuals but also learn to understand the culture and create a more inclusive environment. Sign language can serve as a bridge, enabling better communication between deaf individuals and the wider community," Iwan remarked.

title: Tarakihi catch limits reduce to 10 per person nationwide
content:
Fisheries Minister Shane Jones says tarakihi catch limits will be reduced, with a nationwide recreational fishing limit of 10 per person.
Commercial limits for the eastern fishery are being reduced by 20 percent, and the western fishery by 55 percent.
Jones said he has considered the latest science and catch information, uncertainty about future stocks of young fish, and the effects of use of the fishery in making the decision.
"These measures will immediately reduce fishing pressure on these tarakihi stocks and put them on more positive trajectories, while allowing a lower level of fishing to continue.
Limits have been increased for snapper and trevally on the North Island's east coast, leatherjacket on the South Island's east and south coast, and frostfish and blue mackerel in deep water.
Butterfish catch limits have also been reduced, with a five-per-person recreational limit.
Seafood NZ chief executive Lisa Futschek said the quota management system was working as intended.
"This process matters. Sustainable fisheries management isn't about catch limits remaining static; it is about making changes when the evidence shows they are needed."
The company's general manager for inshore fisheries Tiff Bock said they supported decisions to ensure tarakihi stocks continued to rebuild.
"Industry has been actively rebuilding east coast tarakihi since 2018 through catch reductions, avoidance measures, gear changes, improved monitoring and significant investment in research. We remain committed to rebuilding the stocks."
Reduction 'does not cut it'
Benn Winlove, a spokesperson for the LegaSea non-profit marine life advocacy group, said a 20 percent reduction on the east coast "does not cut it" and the government should expect further court cases.
"We have watched the stock fall dramatically, with little intervention from officials or successive fishery ministers. Court cases by Forest and Bird and the Environmental Law Initiative have made the government make bigger reductions, but it's not working.
"On the east coast, tarakihi is at 7.7 percent of its estimated original biomass. This is well below the 10 percent hard limit where closure is an option, and the rebuild plan is clearly not working."
The Environmental Defence Society (EDS) said tarakihi fared better on the West Coast at 29 percent of its unfished biomass - but it was in rapid decline.
Policy director Raewyn Peart said EDS sought a total closure of the fishery, until the stocks recovered. Seafood New Zealand and other commercial fishing interests sought the 20 percent reduction in the harvest that was adopted by the minister.
"Given how depleted tarakihi stocks are, and how important this fish is for New Zealanders, the minister's decision is extremely disappointing," said Peart.
"EDS called for a complete closure of the fishery given its perilous state. But the minister's decision doesn't even mention closure as an option. This is despite the eastern stock being below the hard limit, which is when closure needs to be considered under the Harvest Strategy Standard," she said.
Fisheries New Zealand's analysis indicated that the harvest reductions adopted by the minister would mean the stocks would continue to be overfished, Peart said.
"It is also clear the western stock will continue to decline and the eastern stock will remain at very low biomass levels for an extended period. This brings the risk that any adverse event, such as a marine heatwave, could tip it over the edge so it never recovers."
"EDS is now investigating legal options to challenge the decision," Peart said.

title: Local leaders have say on reforms to prepare youngsters for work
content:
Local leaders have say on reforms to prepare youngsters for work
Education Secretary convenes leaders from education, industry, and local government at No.10 North to put local expertise at heart of education policies.
Local leaders are to have their say on how to drive excellence across the education system and better prepare young people for work during a summit hosted by the Education Secretary.
Regional mayors, business leaders, headteachers and college principals will convene today (10 September 2026) at No.10 North in Manchester to shape plans to make England a technical education superpower, and ensure technical and academic education are on an equal footing.
It comes following the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) international education rankings earlier in the week – which showed England improved or remained stable against an international backdrop of declining scores and continues to perform significantly above the OECD averages in all 3 subjects. Meanwhile, Estonia shows academic and technical excellence can coexist.
Discussions will focus on the delivery of vocational education reforms from aged 14, work experience opportunities, and making the most of the devolution of billions of pounds of funding for 16 to 19-year-olds.
The meeting will be the first of regular gatherings that will bring together industry, politicians and educators to drive forward reforms. It comes ahead of the publication of the Devolution white paper which will set out plans to give local leaders a greater role in shaping economic growth and opportunity in their areas.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell is set to say in her opening remarks:
I want a new way of working in education. I want change to come not from Whitehall alone, but to be co-designed with those who will deliver it, those who know local strengths and challenges best – you and your colleagues.
That’s what we’re here today, and that’s how I want us to see devolution. I want it to be at the heart of a different way of doing things: a partnership between national government and local areas, so that we can bring the change that children, young people and families need, up and down the country.
The reforms build on the government introducing V levels from aged 16 and expanding T levels from next September to help to tackle the nearly 1 million young people who are not in education, employment or training.
On the same day, Minister Smith will use her first address to the higher education sector at the start of the new term to call on universities to see themselves at the heart of this reform agenda, helping bring growth to every postcode.
Speaking at University UK’s annual conference, she will urge the sector to work with local leaders, colleges, and employers to identify opportunities locally to shape courses and create work experience.
In her speech to university heads, Minister Smith is set to say:
There’s no point building the growth this country desperately needs, if it just embellishes the places that are already prosperous. Growth should spread opportunity and prosperity widely, leaving no area behind.
This vision for widespread growth makes universities’ local connections and contributions just as important as their national and international renown.
Your institutions are a network of economic engines throughout the country. We want to build on your established strengths and successes to distribute opportunity and drive national renewal.
Universities should be at the heart of local partnerships that turn economic opportunity into courses, student workplace experience and good jobs for local people.
This is already happening in areas such as the Humber where the University of Hull works with major local employers including wind turbine manufacturer Siemens Gamesa and renewable energy developer Ørsted. Students can access placements and graduate opportunities, while a master’s degree apprenticeship developed with Siemens Gamesa is training the next generation of offshore wind engineers.
Meanwhile, in the West of England, UWE Bristol and University Centre Weston work with employers including Airbus, Rolls-Royce and GKN Aerospace to deliver engineering degree apprenticeships. Learners combine paid work with degree-level study, while employers help shape training around the skills needed in aerospace and advanced manufacturing.
Chief Executive of the Sixth Form Colleges Association, Bill Watkin, said:
Today’s summit is a very welcome opportunity to discuss how to implement the ambitious reforms set out by the new Prime Minister and Secretary of State.
We share the government’s ambition to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment and training - this is an important national priority that we must all come together to address.
Today could mark the beginning of a new chapter in collaboration between education, industry and government to ensure that every young person can access a high quality pathway to skilled employment or further study.
Chief Executive of the Association of Colleges, David Hughes, said:
The Prime Minister’s has set out a clear and exciting vision of positive pathways for young people through technical education into good jobs from age 14. Those pathways need to go all the way to the highest levels of learning and to open up great careers.
Colleges already contribute so much in this area, and the roundtable is a great opportunity to build the local partnerships needed to scale that work up, with elected mayor’s leading. I’m pleased that the Education Secretary is bringing us all together, there’s a lot to win and a lot to plan for.
Chief Executive of the Confederation of School Trusts, Leora Cruddas CBE said:
I am pleased to be attending this important summit. Public institutions should be understood not simply as mechanisms for delivering services, but as enduring civic assets that generate belonging, trust, and democratic legitimacy.
The strength of a nation depends on the vitality of its local institutions and the relationships between and among them. School trusts in England are civic institutions alongside further education colleges, universities, and NHS trusts, with the capacity to support civic leadership in place.
Amazon UK Country Manager, John Boumphrey, said:
Talent is evenly distributed across this country, but opportunity is not.
At Amazon, around half the people who join our operations teams come either from unemployment or straight from education - including from communities where opportunity is hardest to find.
When you give young people the right support, they thrive. It’s as simple as that. We’re proud to be helping every young person see a real route into a career.

title: Two decades on, Nepal’s conservationists search for new ‘dream’ generation
content:
- In September 2006, a helicopter crash killed 24 people, including then forest minister and senior officials from Nepal’s government and WWF — a day after they handed over a conservation area to resident communities.
- Since the crash, some conservationists say individual roles were replaced, but what was lost was never truly recovered, with visionary leadership growing scarcer since the accident.
- Nepal’s tiger population has more than tripled and forest cover has grown beyond 46%, built on the community forestry model the “lost generation”, but human-wildlife conflict and the emptying of hill villages remain as unresolved conservation issues.
- Devolving control of buffer zones to local communities remains incomplete two decades on, and even the crash’s own commemoration has largely lapsed, leaving current leaders to decide whether to keep running the old conservation model or build a new one.
KATHMANDU — In September 2006, Nepal’s then Minister of Forests and Soil Conservation Gopal Rai and a contingent of conservation leaders flew to a remote village in eastern Nepal to hand over a conservation area to the people living there.
On the evening of Sept. 22, Rai handed over management of the Kanchenjunga Conservation Area (KCA) to the community, hailing it as a milestone in Nepal’s conservation history. “For the community, this was the beginning,” Ghana Shyam Gurung, now WWF’s country representative, tells Mongabay.
The next day, minutes after take-off, the contingent’s Russian-built Mi-8 helicopter crashed, killing all 20 passengers and four crew. Among the dead were the forest minister, his spouse, senior officials, a Finnish diplomat, a senior USAID official and WWF staff. Bad weather hampered rescue efforts for two days. No one in the capital Kathmandu could confirm what had happened until searchers reached the wreckage.
Two decades later, the community-based approach to conservation pioneered by “dreamers” such as Harka and Chandra Gurung and Mingma Norbu Sherpa, all of whom were killed in the crash, still drives Nepal’s wildlife and forest recovery. The country’s tiger population has more than tripled and its forest cover has grown by six percentage points since the crash. But conservationists say progress has since stagnated.
A generation lost
The crash left empty seats at Nepal’s key conservation institutions. Conservationist Sarita Jnawali, then with the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC), remembers the day the deaths were confirmed. “When people like that weren’t there, we felt a huge sense of vacuum,” she tells Mongabay. “It felt like there was nothing left in conservation.”
At the forest ministry, then oint Secretary Krishna Chandra Paudel lost his minister and Acting Secretary Damodar Parajuli. At the Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, ecologist Shiv Raj Bhatta lost his supervisors, director general Narayan Poudel and former director general Tirtha Man Maskey. The two were of such international stature, Bhatta says, that there was no one to replace them, “I wondered how we would ever produce people of that height again.”
WWF lost seven staff, “the single greatest loss of life in WWF’s 45-year history.” Among the dead was Mingma Norbu Sherpa, who had helped establish the Annapurna Conservation Area and led WWF Nepal at the time. “I’m a tough person,” Ghana Shyam Gurung from WWF says. “I could never endure that. That was hard..The hardest thing for me was meeting Mingma sir’s wife — meeting his widow. I haven’t cried that much even for my own mother. That was the first time.”
A wound that left scar
Paudel, who later served as the forest ministry’s secretary before retiring, describes the 20 years as a wound that left a deep scar. “It’s like when parents die suddenly, the family finds some comfort, and carries the ordinary rhythm of life forward,” he tells Mongabay. “But the old loss is never truly fulfilled.”
For Jnawali, the story of the past two decades is one of replacement, not continuity. “The vacuum I imagined didn’t happen, because people from a new generation took over,” she says. “They don’t remember the old story, but the vacuum still got replaced.”
Visionaries and people who dream a dream and see it through have grown scarcer, she says. This could be a result of government instability and weakening individual commitment as much as of the crash itself, she adds.
“In the absence of dreamers who could shift paradigms, what came after 2006 was largely the same work repeated,” she says, referring to the shift from strict, exclusionary conservation to community-based management pioneered and led by the people on the helicopter.
‘Have we stopped dreaming?’
Gurung says the difficult question to answer now is: Have we stopped dreaming after 2006? “We keep talking about the same things, redoing the same work,” he says. “So what’s next? Why aren’t we looking for new green areas?”
Conservation needs a breakthrough on the scale of the 1990s shift to community-based management, he says — one built around climate and water. He points to a model of coexistence suited to a landscape that now holds far more wildlife and far fewer farming families than it did in 2006. “The world ahead is about water,” he says.
Paudel disagrees with Gurung and Jnawali. Forest for Prosperity, the policy vision he says he pushed as secretary to tie conservation to household income, is a new dream by his own account. It aimed at prosperity rather than protection for its own sake. WIt was conservation becoming highly politicized that slowed the sector down, he argues, not that his generation stopped dreaming.
Missed opportunities
Jnawali counts the cost of the crash in missed opportunities for Nepal. Had the 2006 delegation lived, she says she believes that protected areas such as Annapurna and Manaslu might have followed Kanchenjunga into full community management, and new areas might have opened. “We didn’t just lose people that day,” she says. “We lost the pace we were moving at.”
Ecologist Bhatta traces the sector’s shortcomings to a failure of collaboration more than to the crash itself. Nepal’s community-based model won international recognition for biodiversity outcomes, he says. That model included the Terai Arc Landscape approach, a transboundary corridor of protected forests linking Nepal and India. But it delivered less on livelihoods, he says, because other ministries never fully joined in.
He says he wants devolution and to hand more control from the government to local communities. Buffer zones, areas around national parks, should be transferred more completely to community control, he says, with the park warden no longer the central authority. “The core was always local people,” he adds. That handover, in his view, is unfinished business.
Success in numbers
Nepal’s tiger population has grown from 121 in 2010 to a record 429 this year. Its rhino population has grown from 645 in 2015 to 752 in 2021. “We’ve increased tigers, we’ve increased rhinos,” former Secretary of the Ministry of Forests Paudel says. “That’s a result of the dream that generation was dreaming at the time.”
Part of that recovery rests on the community forestry system that the 2006 generation helped build. Nepal’s forest cover has grown from about 40% in the 1990s to more than 46% today — one of the sharpest reversals of deforestation anywhere. More than 23,000 community forest user groups now manage roughly 2.5 million hectares (6.2 million acres), and about a third of Nepal’s population belongs to one.
The cost of success
The recovering wildlife itself has become part of the strain. As tiger and rhino numbers have climbed, so has the toll of people killed or injured by the animals brought back by conservation efforts.
A 2026 study of Nepal’s Terai Arc Landscape documented 245 tiger attacks on humans between 2010 and 2024 with 141 fatalities. The study also found a sharp surge in attacks in the Banke-Bardia complex between 2019 and 2023 — Bardia’s tiger population roughly doubled over the same period. Attacks declined after park authorities captured and relocated 21 tigers responsible for repeated conflicts, the study says.
Meanwhile, in the hills, people are abandoning their villages. In Taplejung, the district where the 2006 helicopter went down, data from officials in its Phungling Municipality reportedly say 245 to 330 families leave hill settlements every year with most citing crop losses due to monkeys.
A memory fading
In 2006 after the last rites of the deceased were performed and work resumed, the government instituted the National Conservation Day and a National Conservation Award to commemorate the memory of the deceased. WWF set up memorial scholarships that have since supported around 200 students, many of them women from underserved communities. More than 20 memorial scholars have gone on to pursue master’s degrees in New Zealand, according to WWF’s Gurung.
Two decades on, even the memory of the crash is fading unevenly. In Taplejung, a memorial features statue of the 24 deceased. In Kathmandu, the government-built statue park in Ramkot is overgrown and dilapidated, some names faded or gone. Paudel says observance of the disaster, once marked at the highest level of government, has all but lapsed. “Twenty years have passed and we have almost abandoned it for the last 10,” he says.
Local problems demand local solutions
Paudel says some progress has been made in tackling the challenges, but the measures don’t address the challenges completely. He points to compensation schemes for human-wildlife conflict deaths and insurance programs, both introduced since 2006, but argues that the answers Nepal needs next won’t come from Kathmandu. “Local governments should look for local solutions,” he says. “People know better.”

title: Rescatistas devolvieron a su dueña dinero hallado entre los escombros de Residencias Caribe, en La Guaira
content:
Entre los restos de las Residencias Caribe, en La Guaira, voluntarios encontraron dinero mientras avanzaban en labores de búsqueda y recuperación de pertenencias. En lugar de incorporarlo entre los objetos recuperados, decidieron localizar a su dueña y devolvérselo.
El hallazgo fue protagonizado por integrantes del equipo de rescate Máquina de Hierro, quienes contactaron a una mujer que permanecía en el lugar en busca de su esposo. El momento de la entrega quedó registrado en un video publicado por la periodista Maryorin Méndez, que compartió el diálogo entre los rescatistas y la afectada.
"Nosotros acabamos de encontrarte un dinero aquí abajo, mi vida. Queremos hacerte la entrega de este dinero", le dice uno de los voluntarios mientras le muestra los billetes recuperados entre los restos de la estructura.
Los rescatistas también habían encontrado documentos, prendas y otros objetos personales. Durante la conversación explicaron que fueron separando las pertenencias que aparecían durante la remoción para entregarlas a sus propietarios o familiares.
La mujer rompió en llanto al recibir el dinero y explicó que no se trataba de una suma cualquiera. Había pasado un año reuniendo esos ahorros con la intención de iniciar un negocio.
“Nosotros íbamos a empezar esa misma semana del 24, estuve parada un año guardando, guardando, guardando, para salir adelante y tener mi propio negocio”, contó.
Los voluntarios insistieron en que querían devolverle todo lo que pudiera recuperarse.
“Todo lo que salga de aquí está en ellos” le explicaron, mientras continuaban revisando los restos en busca de documentos y objetos que pudieran pertenecer a las familias afectadas.
Labores de rescate continúan tres meses después de los terremotos
El episodio ocurrió casi tres meses después de los terremotos del 24 de junio que devastaron zonas de La Guaira y dejaron miles de víctimas y cientos de estructuras colapsadas. El paso del tiempo no ha significado el cierre de las labores en todos los puntos afectados: en Caribe todavía permanecen equipos dedicados a la remoción y búsqueda de víctimas y pertenencias.
Este lunes, por ejemplo, voluntarios del Campamento Madrid reportaron que mantienen las labores de rescate y remoción de escombros en la zona. El grupo reúne a 29 rescatistas procedentes de otros lugares del país.
La búsqueda no se limita a los restos humanos. A medida que se remueve el material de las edificaciones destruidas aparecen documentos, fotografías, ropa y otros objetos que alguna vez formaron parte de la vida cotidiana de quienes habitaban esos edificios. La magnitud de los escombros ha convertido su clasificación y retiro en uno de los grandes desafíos de la recuperación.

title: Sustainability, Vol. 18, Pages 9749: Introducing Earthquake Preparedness from Early Childhood: The “Earthy and Quaky” Education Program as an Interdisciplinary and Learning Pathway Toward a Culture of Safety
content: Destructive earthquakes are natural hazards highlighting the importance of introducing disaster preparedness from early childhood. Preschool children require developmentally appropriate educational approaches that connect scientific understanding with experiential, play-based, and participatory learning. This study presents the design and implementation of the “Earthy and Quaky” (EQ) earthquake education program, developed for children aged 3–6 years and implemented in two preschool educational settings in Zografou City (Attica, Greece). The program was structured as an interdisciplinary and progressive learning pathway comprising eight thematic units integrating natural and social sciences, language, mathematics, music and movement, visual arts, puppet theater, simulation, and earthquake drills. Follow-up activities and family involvement extended learning beyond the classroom. The implementation involved 28 children, whose participation, verbal responses, interactions, behavioral responses, and drawings were qualitatively observed. The observations indicated active engagement with concepts, including the Earth’s structure, earthquake occurrence and impact, and self-protection practices. Within the context of this small-scale implementation, the observations indicate that an interdisciplinary, experiential, and activity-based framework can provide a supportive learning context for earthquake preparedness during preschool years. The adaptable structure, low-cost materials, repeated reinforcement, and school–family connection may offer potential for adaptation to other preschool contexts after studying applicability and effectiveness with larger and more diverse samples.

title: From eviction fears to land titles: Andhra Pradesh will regularise thousands of Vizag homes
content:
From eviction fears to land titles: Andhra Pradesh will regularise thousands of Vizag homes
According to officials, the estimated market value of the encroached land is Rs 8,800 crore. The house-site title deeds will be distributed to the families on September 19, officials said.
The extent of encroachment over vast parcels of expensive government land has meant that successive governments — including the previous Chandrababu Naidu regime — have been reluctant to regularise these constructions for fear of encouraging more illegal constructions. (File)
In an unusual move, the Andhra Pradesh government has decided to regularise over 26,000 unauthorised houses on government land in Visakhapatnam— a development that marks a significant departure from successive governments’ stance.
According to officials, the estimated market value of the encroached land is Rs 8,800 crore. The house-site title deeds will be distributed to the families on September 19, officials said.
“The wait spanning decades is coming to an end… The dream of thousands of families to secure rights over their homes is on the verge of becoming reality. Every family dreams of having their own home with full ownership rights. To the thousands of poor families who have built homes on government land and lived there for years. We are granting you rights over your homes and fulfilling the dreams of 28,445 families. Across 11 mandals, we are regularising 1,933,853 square yards of land worth Rs 8,874 crore and issuing titles for house sites,” Naidu said in a statement.
For those who fought to keep their land, the move brings relief. B Anantha Lakshmi, head of a committee which fought for the rights in Gajuwaka, said these families can finally sleep well. Some 5,597 houses are being regularised in Gajuwaka.
“The threat of being evicted and our precious homes demolished was always there. The families can finally be at ease. When they constructed the houses decades ago, many were deceived into buying after being told it was private property. Some built rudimentary houses as they had nowhere else to go. Our children grew up here…there was nowhere else to go if they had taken this away,” she said.
Additionally, the government said some 24,000 families were likely to get a similar benefit.
Revenue Minister A Satya Prasad said the houses were being given on “compassionate grounds” and came at a time when “governments are demolishing illegal constructions on government lands and seizing them”.
“Our government’s policy is that no poor family should remain without a house. There should never be a situation where a poor family does not have a roof over their heads,” he said.
This is a departure from the government’s previous stance. The extent of encroachment over vast parcels of expensive government land has meant that successive governments — including the previous Chandrababu Naidu regime — have been reluctant to regularise these constructions for fear of encouraging more illegal constructions. In the past, governments are also stated to have explored the option of taking back and auctioning the land but decided against it amid the possibility of litigation.

title: Community-based conservation is a good climate investment in Brazil & beyond (commentary)
content:
- In Brazil, community-based land management of collective territories has produced striking results for conservation.
- The social situation of these communities is less encouraging, though, with nearly half of households living a precarious existence, suggesting income-transfer programs linked to conservation, like the Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF), could make a difference — if implemented well.
- “Community-based conservation, with its proven effectiveness, would be a compelling focus [for] this type of investment, especially in Brazil,” a new op-ed argues.
- This article is a commentary. The views expressed are those of the authors, not necessarily of Mongabay.
More than half a century has passed since Garrett Hardin published The Tragedy of the Commons in Science in 1968. In that influential article, he argued that human greed and short-term thinking would drive societies toward collapse. Hardin illustrated his argument with the well-known example of herders sharing a pasture: each herder would receive all the income from adding another animal, while the cost of consuming the grass would be shared by all. The path toward pasture depletion was therefore set, as some herders would keep adding animals for their own benefit rather than restrain themselves in the name of an abstract collective good. For Hardin, there was no way to change this equation; the solution for the sustainability of life on the planet was population control.
Two decades later, and not by chance, it was a woman who challenged this foretold tragedy, showing that, under certain conditions, human beings can be organized and perceptive enough to cooperate and avert collective failure. Elinor Ostrom developed a theory of cooperation applied to the use of common-pool resources, explaining how locally agreed rules can enable shared benefits. It was an expression of confidence in human social intelligence.
The point is not to decide who was right or wrong. Hardin’s argument helps us understand why reducing greenhouse gas emissions remains so difficult, as do countless examples of the degradation of humanity’s natural heritage and, consequently, of the foundations of our future. Ostrom, in turn, helps explain many successful cases of collective natural resource management — also known as community-based management or conservation — led by the people who live in the places where resources are used.
Collective management arrangements depend on clearly defined geographical boundaries, locally agreed rules for decision-making and conflict resolution, monitoring, and graduated sanctions. Behind these formal arrangements, Ostrom also recognized the importance of factors such as familiarity among members, frequent interactions, shared identity, mutual trust, and reciprocity.
This theoretical framework on cooperation and natural resource use, developed by sociologists, economists, and political scientists through observation of real-world cases, is highly significant. Around 40% of the world’s protected areas are under community-based management by Indigenous peoples and traditional communities, conserving at least one-third of global biodiversity.
In Brazil, community management of collective territories has also produced striking results. Despite intense pressures, over the past 30 years Indigenous lands have lost, at the national scale, just over 1.2% of their natural cover, Quilombola territories, managed by Afro-Brazilian communities descended from formerly enslaved persons, have lost 4.7%, while private areas have lost 17-19.9% based on those same reports.
Brazil’s National System of Conservation Units (SNUC), which governs the management of the country’s parks and reserves, formally recognizes traditional communities for their conservation performance and sustainable use of natural resources, as well as for their territorial and cultural rights. Established in 2000, the SNUC recognizes extractive reserves (Resex) as official categories within the national system: public territories reserved for the exclusive use of the communities that live there and depend on, manage, and conserve natural resources.
Resex emerged from the struggle led by Chico Mendes and his fellow rubber tappers for forest-based agrarian reform in the Brazilian state of Acre. Their demands were later supported by those of fishers, babassu coconut breakers, and other traditional communities, who raised their voices and made their conservation practices visible, demonstrating their need for access to natural resources and gaining recognition in public policy.
Today, Brazil has 98 Resex, covering 15.7 million hectares (nearly 39 million acres), an area nearly twice the size of Scotland. These territories are co-managed by local communities and the Brazilian state through management councils that represent local actors and have deliberative authority. Managing these protected areas therefore requires both government and communities to understand territorial realities, histories of struggle, social organization, the structure of the state and its institutions, ecosystem ecology, the dynamics of natural resource use, and, critically, the art and science of collective organization.
The social situation of these communities, however, is less encouraging. According to Brazil’s 2022 national census, 315,833 people live in sustainable-use conservation units such as Resex, excluding environmental protection areas (APA). Among them, 40% face some form of precariousness, whether related to sanitation or water supply, a finding that points to the potential reach of income-transfer programs linked to conservation.
Among public responses to poverty in protected areas, the Bolsa Verde Program stands out. Created in 2011 and inspired by the Bolsa Família Program, Bolsa Verde paid 300 reais ($58) per quarter to around 100,000 families until it was discontinued in 2016. In 2023, the program was relaunched with higher payments, a broader target population, and nationwide coverage: quarterly payments rose to 600 reais (just over $116) per family for beneficiaries in collective territories of Indigenous peoples and traditional communities.
Through adhesion terms, community members commit to complying with environmental legislation, maintaining vegetation cover and biodiversity conservation in the territories served, taking part in environmental conservation activities, and following territorial management instruments such as use plans, management plans, and fishing agreements. From 2023 to 2025, the program recorded 32,800 beneficiary families in 71 conservation units across the country.
Findings from a 2021 literature review of community-based conservation arrangements show the power of community management to deliver combined environmental and social outcomes. The study reviewed 3,100 publications on the performance of collective-management arrangements, identifying those that provided evidence of environmental outcomes, social outcomes, and the relationships between the two. This resulted in 169 publications containing all three types of evidence. Their analysis showed that local governance arrangements achieved combined environmental and social success in 56% of cases, while arrangements centralized in external management bodies did so in only 16%.
The multiple benefits of community-based conservation, together with the scale which Brazil has achieved through these initiatives, could make an important contribution to global forest-based climate finance. The Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF), coordinated by Brazil and launched at the COP30 climate summit in 2025, aims to raise more than $10 billion to reward countries that keep forests standing. With its operation scheduled to begin in 2027, participating countries have not yet identified the beneficiaries of these investments, leaving transparency gaps, and missing an opportunity to strengthen fundraising around potential results.
Community-based conservation, with its proven effectiveness, would be a compelling focus for fundraising and a deserving priority for this type of investment, especially in Brazil.
Ana Cristina Barros is a graduate student at the National School of Tropical Botany of the Rio de Janeiro Botanical Garden. title: “Un kilómetro de humanidad”, la propuesta de un arquitecto mexicano presentada en El Salvador
content:
“Un kilómetro de humanidad”, la propuesta de un arquitecto mexicano presentada en El Salvador
El arquitecto mexicano Rafael Hernández Monroy presentó en el Foro Mundial de la Bicicleta una reflexión que busca cambiar la manera de entender la movilidad. Te contamos los detalles
Un kilómetro son 1,000 metros. La medida no cambia, pero recorrer esa distancia puede convertirse en una experiencia completamente diferente dependiendo de quién lo haga.
Esa premisa llevó al arquitecto mexicano Rafael Hernández Monroy a plantear una pregunta aparentemente sencilla, ¿cuánto mide un kilómetro de humanidad?
El profesional llevó trajo esa interrogante hasta El Salvador, donde participó en el Foro Mundial de la Bicicleta para compartir su experiencia en urbanismo y algunos de los proyectos desarrollados en México.
Su propuesta parte de colocar a las personas en el centro de la planificación de las ciudades. Un niño que camina hacia la escuela, un adulto mayor, una persona que utiliza silla de ruedas o alguien que se desplaza en bicicleta pueden recorrer el mismo kilómetro, pero las condiciones de la calle determinarán qué tan difícil, seguro o accesible resulta hacerlo.
Elementos tan cotidianos como disponer de un cruce seguro, encontrar árboles que proporcionen sombra, contar con un espacio para descansar o poder desplazarse sin temor terminan cambiando la experiencia.
“Siempre se ha enfocado el desarrollo en creer que entre más infraestructura construyamos, entre más le entreguemos nuestra ciudad al automóvil, es desarrollo”, explicó Hernández Monroy a elsalvador.com.
Para él, la prioridad debería ser distinta. “La ciudad debe ser para el peatón”, sostuvo.
Entre las soluciones que plantea están la construcción de aceras seguras, ciclovías y zonas peatonales, pero también un cambio en la forma en que ciudadanos y autoridades imaginan los espacios que ya existen.
De un camellón a un parque lineal
Durante su participación en el Foro Mundial de la Bicicleta, Hernández Monroy mostró ejemplos de los denominados “imaginarios urbanos” que ha desarrollado en Atlacomulco. La idea consiste en tomar fotografías de espacios reales y, mediante representaciones digitales, mostrar cómo podrían transformarse aplicando otras propuestas urbanísticas.
Uno de los ejemplos presentados corresponde a un camellón que actualmente divide una vialidad y que, bajo esa propuesta conceptual, podría convertirse en un parque lineal con áreas para caminar, utilizar la bicicleta y encontrarse con otras personas.
No se trata únicamente de mostrar una imagen atractiva, explicó, sino de provocar una conversación entre los habitantes sobre las posibilidades de transformar su entorno.
“Siempre nos conformamos con lo mismo de siempre, pero ya vimos que podemos tener una mejor ciudad”, comentó al explicar el propósito de estos ejercicios.
La experiencia que originó la pregunta
“Kilómetros de Humanidad”, sin embargo, no nació únicamente de su trabajo como arquitecto. La idea comenzó durante un viaje que Hernández Monroy realizaba por Centroamérica. Se encontraba en Costa Rica y pretendía llegar por tierra hasta Guatemala, pero al arribar a la frontera con Nicaragua descubrió que necesitaba una visa para ingresar.
Ante la imposibilidad de continuar inmediatamente, decidió caminar desde la frontera hacia el poblado costarricense de Los Chiles.
Durante el recorrido encontró un puesto de atención a refugiados de UNICEF, donde, según relató, le proporcionaron comida, agua, internet e incluso le ofrecieron hospedaje. Finalmente, él tuvo una alternativa, regresar a San José, comprar un boleto de avión y continuar su viaje.
Otras personas que encontró durante aquella experiencia no tenían esa posibilidad. Esa diferencia cambió la forma en que comenzó a pensar las distancias.
Mientras para él desplazarse era consecuencia de una decisión personal y disponía de recursos para modificar su ruta, para otras personas recorrer cientos o miles de kilómetros puede estar relacionado con situaciones como violencia, pobreza o desplazamiento. Fue entonces cuando la medida física dejó de ser suficiente.
¿Cuánta humanidad cabe en un kilómetro?
Con el tiempo, el propio arquitecto reformuló la pregunta que dio nombre a su proyecto. “La pregunta real creo que siempre estuvo mal hecha. No es cuánto mide un kilómetro de Humanidad, es cuánta humanidad se puede instaurar en un kilómetro”, afirmó.
Para Hernández Monroy, la respuesta puede encontrarse observando cómo se construye una calle y preguntándose quiénes realmente pueden utilizarla. Una acera demasiado estrecha, por ejemplo, puede representar un obstáculo para cualquier peatón y convertirse directamente en una barrera para alguien que utiliza silla de ruedas.
Lo mismo ocurre con los entornos escolares. El arquitecto plantea pensar en espacios suficientemente seguros para facilitar que los niños puedan desplazarse entre sus viviendas y centros educativos.
Durante su visita, Hernández Monroy también destacó la recuperación de espacios públicos que observó en San Salvador y consideró que la realización del Foro Mundial de la Bicicleta contribuye a colocar en la discusión regional formas de movilidad distintas al automóvil.
Al final, su propuesta plantea otra manera de evaluar el desarrollo urbano, no observar solamente cuánta infraestructura tiene una ciudad, sino preguntarse para quién fue construida. “Cuando hablamos de ciudadanos hablamos de todos”, resumió.
