title: Alberi per trattenere l’azoto e tecniche di semina intelligenti: così gli agricoltori della Tanzania si stanno adattando alle precipitazioni imprevedibili
content:
Alberi per trattenere l’azoto e tecniche di semina intelligenti: così gli agricoltori della Tanzania si stanno adattando alle precipitazioni imprevedibili
Indice
A Udumka la risposta alle piogge che arrivano male, troppo forti o tutte insieme sta crescendo dentro un vivaio. La comunità del sud della Tanzania ha cominciato a coltivare specie capaci di trattenere acqua e fissare l’azoto, inserendole in terreni messi alla prova dalle coltivazioni intensive e dalle precipitazioni che possono trascinare via i nutrienti. Nessuna tecnologia futuriatica. Qui si piantano alberi.
Il vivaio è gestito dall’Udumka Environmental Group, collettivo locale coinvolto nel progetto Her Resilience, Our Planet. La scelta delle specie serve a recuperare gradualmente fertilità e a rendere i campi meno fragili davanti a un clima diventato più irregolare. A lavorarci ci sono anche formatori scelti e preparati all’interno della comunità, così le conoscenze non rimangono appese all’arrivo di tecnici esterni. È uno degli interventi raccontati da CARE Tanzania, che partecipa al progetto.
Gli alberi entrano nei campi
Gli alberi azotofissatori lavorano soprattutto sottoterra. Grazie alla relazione con alcuni batteri presenti nelle radici, contribuiscono a rendere disponibile nel sistema agricolo l’azoto atmosferico, uno dei nutrienti essenziali per le piante. Nel tempo entrano in gioco anche foglie, radici e materia organica lasciata sul terreno.
È un principio usato da tempo nei sistemi agroforestali e documentato anche dalla FAO: alberi e colture possono condividere lo stesso spazio agricolo, con effetti sulla fertilità del terreno, sulla gestione dell’acqua e sulla protezione del suolo. A Udumka questa vecchia idea agricola viene rimessa al lavoro dentro un problema molto contemporaneo.
Le piogge, infatti, sono diventate più difficili da prevedere. CARE descrive precipitazioni violente, grandine e allagamenti capaci di compromettere i raccolti e impoverire ulteriormente terreni già sfruttati. Piantare una specie adatta, qui, significa cercare di lasciare qualcosa nel terreno anche quando l’acqua porta via il resto.
A pochi chilometri, cambiano anche le patate
Nel vicino villaggio di Kihesa Mgagao, Bariki Kagine coltivava patate con risultati scarsi e raccolti particolarmente vulnerabili alla grandine. Poi ha cominciato a cambiare diverse cose insieme: la distanza tra le piante, il momento della semina, l’uso delle previsioni meteorologiche, la fertilizzazione, la gestione dei parassiti e perfino la varietà coltivata. Ha scelto la Sagitta, più adatta al suo terreno. Il raccolto ottenuto gli ha fruttato circa 2 milioni di scellini tanzaniani, secondo quanto riportato da CARE.
È il risultato di un solo agricoltore, ma il cambiamento si vede bene: spostare una semina, lasciare più spazio tra le piante, scegliere una varietà diversa può fare la differenza quando il calendario delle piogge smette di comportarsi come prima. E infatti l’adattamento, da queste parti, ha un aspetto piuttosto poco spettacolare. Un albero nel posto giusto. Una patata piantata qualche giorno dopo. Un agricoltore che guarda le previsioni prima di entrare nel campo.
Il progetto punta a coinvolgere oltre 60 mila piccoli agricoltori
Her Resilience, Our Planet lavora nel bacino del Great Ruaha River, una delle aree agricole e naturali più importanti della Tanzania meridionale. Il programma è sostenuto anche da Global Affairs Canada e, secondo la scheda ufficiale del Governo canadese, proseguirà fino al 2030. CARE indica tra gli obiettivi oltre 60.000 piccoli agricoltori e 18.000 imprenditori agricoli coinvolti nella regione, con particolare attenzione a donne e giovani. Sono traguardi previsti dal progetto, non persone già raggiunte.
Per ora la storia è molto più piccola, ed è probabilmente per questo che funziona. Un vivaio gestito dal villaggio. Alberi scelti anche per ciò che fanno al terreno. Un agricoltore che cambia il modo di coltivare le patate e riesce a venderle meglio. Da Udumka non arriva una soluzione pronta per qualsiasi campo africano. Arriva qualcosa di più concreto: mentre il clima cambia le regole, questa comunità sta cambiando il modo di stare sul terreno. A volte cominciando da un albero.
Ti potrebbe interessare anche:
- Nei villaggi della Tanzania la crisi climatica si combatte con alveari, pollai e donne finalmente ammesse alle decisioni
- La crisi climatica si manifesta in modo differente in ciascun Paese: la campagna globale del clima nata dal basso e diffusa via Whatsapp
- In Burkina Faso hanno lasciato decidere alle donne come spendere i soldi per il clima: ora usano il 30% di legna in meno

title: No more book bans: how Florida students are pushing rightwingers out of school boards
content:
Jimmy Glover’s youngest children were in high school when he noticed their Florida school district taking an unsettling turn. Beloved books were being pulled from shelves. Teachers were scared of being targeted.
“There was this culture of fear that was permeating throughout the district,” Glover said of Sarasota county.
By channeling anger against mask mandates in schools, the rightwing group Moms for Liberty, founded in Florida, built an outsized influence on school boards across the country in 2022. Soon, members began pressuring schools to remake their curricula along conservative ideological lines, erasing mentions of LGBTQ+ Americans, slavery, racism and more.
As a Black dad living in a historically Black part of Sarasota, Glover said he was especially disturbed by governor Ron DeSantis’s announcement that Florida schools would begin teaching students that some Black people benefited from slavery. “Now my children and the students in my community weren’t going to be learning about the true history of this country,” Glover said.
So the father of four decided to run for Sarasota’s school board this year. He is part of a larger movement of students, parents, teachers and concerned community members pushing back against the influence of groups like Moms for Liberty in Florida public education. They wanted schools that were safe and welcoming for all students, and that focused on learning rather than scoring points on the national political scene.
And last month, they won.
Progressive candidates beat opponents backed by or aligned with Moms for Liberty in school board races across the state – in many cases reversing gains made by the group in 2022. Of the 30 candidates the group supported that year, 20 have declined to seek re-election, have been defeated or will face runoffs in November, according to the LGBTQ+ rights group Equality Florida.
In Sarasota, home to Moms for Liberty’s cofounder Bridget Ziegler, progressives flipped the school board, with liberal candidates Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry replacing more conservative members (school board races in Florida are technically nonpartisan). Glover got more votes than either of his conservative opponents, but his race will go to a runoff in November since no candidate won a majority.
When reached for comment, Moms for Liberty referred the Guardian to a public statement disputing the notion that the recent Florida election represented a loss for the group: “Moms for Liberty-endorsed school board candidates won or advanced in 11 of 15 races across Florida.” But the group had issued fewer endorsements than in past elections and declined to endorse any candidate in several counties. That included Sarasota county, where board chair Ziegler, who has been plagued by scandal, was not running for re-election.
Meanwhile, organizers for Glover’s campaign and others say the elections in Florida mark a turning point, a rejection of rightwing educational ideology in a deep-red part of a deep-red state. And, they say, the victories hold lessons for progressives campaigning on the national stage in the midterms and beyond.
“We know that a better future is possible,” said Sebastian Martinez, president of the Sarasota Next Gen Democrats, a youth organizing group that helped campaign for the county’s progressive slate. “We’ll work every day to get there.”
Students step up and organize
Glover wasn’t the only Florida parent concerned about the influence of Moms for Liberty over his children’s education. The group had success in 2022 by appealing to voters angry about pandemic school closures, and by joining the larger rightwing campaign against “critical race theory”. But Moms for Liberty’s popularity has waned since then, said Liv Coleman, a professor of political science and international studies at the University of Tampa.
By the time Stephanie Vanos ran for Orange county’s school board in 2024, the top question voters asked her was: “Are you the one who wants to ban books?”
“It speaks to the outrage at state censorship in our schools and the complete disrespect for the first amendment,” said Vanos, who won her seat that year.
But that outrage had yet to be fully harnessed.
Martinez, now 22, has been active in school board organizing since he was 16. He started Next Gen Democrats last year as a way to expand young Sarasotans’ role in Democratic politics. “I really wanted to see young people not just get involved in organizing, but to become part of the party,” he said.
For youth, one barrier to political participation is money, Martinez said – they can’t afford to volunteer their time when they could be working a paid job. So to help recruit and retain young canvassers, the group offered $20 an hour. “The Democratic party is supposed to be a party of working-class people supporting working-class people, and so it only makes sense to then pay people to work,” Martinez said.
Sarasota Next Gen Democrats recruited about 20 high school students to phone bank, knock on doors and distribute yard signs around the county, said Kennedy Cole, the group’s political director. They also helped decorate a school bus that drove around Sarasota on Election Day, getting the word out about progressive candidates.
Students “were sick of what we’ve seen from our school board, and we knew that Megan, Beth and Jimmy would help return normalcy to it”, said Cole, a 17-year-old high school senior. “Students really worked their butts off to get those results.”
It wasn’t just students. Youth organizers met regularly with other community activists, including a group of retired women who sent 7,000 handwritten postcards to Sarasota voters. A parents’ group invited candidates to a local park to meet voters while their kids played. Equality Florida spent $250,000 on mailers in support of candidates around the state who were facing opponents aligned with Moms for Liberty.
“In order to do something like this, it takes a web of people,” Cole said. “It’s a lot of different people operating in their own ways.”
‘Tired of the chaos’
Whether they were knocking on doors or meeting families at the playground, winning candidates spread a back-to-basics message that resonated with voters across political lines. Cole likes to tell the story of a close friend whose conservative parents voted for liberal school board candidates “because they were tired of the chaos” that Moms for Liberty had brought.
Sarasota schools’ statewide ranking had slipped since conservative activists took control of the school board, said Mayberry, a former teacher who won a seat representing Sarasota’s fifth district. “The focus came off of academic performance,” Mayberry said.
She and other successful candidates campaigned to restore that focus. They ran on issues like school funding, academic achievement and support for teachers and students, Coleman said. “They really just focused on things that affected people’s everyday lives.”
That approach could be instructive for candidates around the country, in November and beyond. Sarasota Next Gen Democrats and their allies built a movement that was “not right v left, not parents v students, not students v teachers”, Cole said. “We were able to organize as a community coalition of people who were sick and tired of political games being played with our students and our education, and want a better change for the future.”
That future includes continuing to campaign for Glover, who will face Republican-backed candidate Heidi Brandt in a runoff election in November. If Glover wins, he would be the first person of color ever to serve on the Sarasota county school board. He’ll also have his work cut out for him in a district reeling from book ban battles and facing funding cuts as a statewide school voucher program pulls money from public schools.
“We have a big challenge coming up,” he said. “We’re coming out of a time when culture wars and personal agendas dominated the headlines, so we have a lot of work to do.”
But he and the organizers behind him are optimistic – not just about Sarasota, but about the country as a whole.
“If it can happen here,” Martinez said of the victories this August, “it can happen anywhere.”

title: Phillip Island removed foxes; little penguin colony grew from 12,000 to 40,000
content:
Phillip Island’s little penguins once faced a crisis that threatened to erase much of their presence from the island. By the 1980s, nine of its 10 penguin colonies had disappeared, while the final colony on the Summerland Peninsula was also under pressure from introduced predators, habitat loss and human activity. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, a long-running conservation effort combining fox control, habitat restoration, scientific research and land rehabilitation helped reverse that decline. The surviving little-penguin population grew from about 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today. The story, detailed in the organisation’s pest-control, research and history records, shows how protecting wildlife often requires more than removing a single threat—it demands sustained cooperation between scientists, governments, local communities and visitors. Read on to know more:
A predator that changed the island
Phillip Island, also known as Milawul, is famous for the nightly arrival of little penguins at the Penguin Parade. Yet the sight that attracts visitors today was once at risk of disappearing.
Red foxes were introduced to Phillip Island in the early 1900s. Over time, they became one of the most serious threats to the island’s wildlife. Little penguins are especially vulnerable because they spend much of their lives at sea but return to land to breed, moult and raise their chicks. Their nests are often located in burrows or sheltered areas close to the coast, where they can be exposed to predators.
Phillip Island Nature Parks describes foxes as the little penguins’ biggest threat on land. By the 1980s, nine of the island’s 10 penguin colonies had become extinct. The remaining colony on the Summerland Peninsula, which includes the Penguin Parade, was also under threat.
The decline was not caused by foxes alone. Research identified several other pressures, including habitat destruction, housing development, traffic near penguin colonies, fire and domestic pets. Together, these threats made it increasingly difficult for penguins to survive and breed successfully.
Warning signs from research
The island’s conservation response was shaped by research. Population studies conducted during the 1980s showed that the last remaining penguin colony could disappear by the late 1990s if existing threats continued.
That warning encouraged authorities and conservation groups to take action. The Penguin Protection Plan, announced in 1985, included scientific research, habitat management, a fox-control program and the gradual buyback of houses in the Summerland Estate.
The housing estate had been built within the penguins’ habitat. As houses, roads and associated infrastructure were removed, the land could be returned to a more natural condition. This was a major undertaking and required years of planning, funding and rehabilitation.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says the buyback and removal of the Summerland Estate continued for decades, as per reports. The final houses and infrastructure were removed in 2010, after which an ongoing rehabilitation program was established to help penguins and other wildlife thrive.
This approach recognised an important conservation principle: removing a predator is not enough if the habitat remains unsafe. Wildlife needs places to shelter, feed, breed and raise young without constant disturbance.
The campaign against foxes
Fox control began as a coordinated effort involving farmers, rangers and conservation workers. According to Phillip Island Nature Parks, more than 1,000 foxes were removed over a period of 20 years.
The organisation initiated a dedicated Fox Eradication Project in 2006. Rather than relying on one method, the project used an integrated approach involving different techniques to locate and remove foxes across the island.
The goal was ambitious. Instead of simply reducing fox numbers, conservation teams aimed to remove foxes from Phillip Island altogether. This was important because even a small number of predators could threaten vulnerable colonies and prevent other species from recovering.
The campaign required persistent monitoring. Rangers and other workers had to search for signs of foxes, respond to sightings and prevent the animals from re-establishing a population. The work also formed part of wider pest management on the island, including programs targeting feral and roaming cats and rabbits.
In 2017, Phillip Island was declared fox-free after an intensive 20-year eradication program. The campaign was supported by the Victorian Government, Penguin Parade visitors, the Penguin Foundation and the Helen Macpherson Smith Trust.
Habitat restoration made a difference
The recovery of the little penguins was closely connected to the restoration of their habitat.
The Summerland Peninsula had once been transformed by housing development and human activity. Removing the houses allowed conservation teams to rebuild a landscape better suited to wildlife. The rehabilitation work helped restore vegetation, reduce disturbance and create safer areas for nesting.
The return of natural habitat also benefited species beyond little penguins. Short-tailed shearwaters and other coastal birds use the island’s protected areas, while the fox-free environment later supported the reintroduction of eastern barred bandicoots.
In 2017, the same year Phillip Island was declared fox-free, researchers released eastern barred bandicoots onto the Summerland Peninsula. The area had been rehabilitated from a former housing estate into a natural environment that supported a thriving little-penguin colony and migratory short-tailed shearwaters.
This illustrates how conservation gains can extend across an ecosystem. Protecting one habitat can create opportunities for several threatened species, especially when predators are controlled and human disturbance is reduced.
From 12,000 to 40,000 penguins
Phillip Island Nature Parks reports that extensive conservation work helped increase the number of little penguins from approximately 12,000 in the mid-1980s to an estimated 40,000 today.
The figures represent more than a simple population increase. They reflect the combined effect of predator control, habitat restoration, reduced development pressure, scientific monitoring and community involvement.
The Penguin Parade also provides a useful way to monitor changes. Guides count the number of penguins crossing the beach each night, and annual averages can offer insight into population trends. These counts do not represent every penguin on the island, but they help researchers track changes in the colony over time.
Conservation teams also monitor breeding success by studying the number of chicks fledged per breeding pair at selected sites. This helps researchers understand not only how many penguins return to land, but also whether they are successfully reproducing.
Such long-term monitoring is essential because wildlife populations can change in response to food availability, disease, weather, marine conditions, human activity and other factors. Regular data collection allows managers to identify problems early and adjust conservation strategies.
Research continues on land and sea
Although the fox eradication campaign was a major achievement, the work of protecting little penguins has not ended.
Phillip Island Nature Parks says its researchers study penguins in both terrestrial and marine environments. This is necessary because little penguins spend around 80 per cent of their time at sea, even though they depend on land for breeding.
Researchers use GPS trackers and other devices to study where penguins travel for food. Tracking has shown that many penguins feed within 50 kilometres of the island’s colony, while some individuals travel farther during winter, including towards Portland in Victoria and Port Phillip Bay near Melbourne.
Understanding these movements helps scientists identify potential threats in the marine environment. Changes in ocean temperature, prey availability, pollution and human activity can all affect the penguins’ ability to find food.
Research projects also examine feeding hotspots by combining information about where penguins go, how much they eat and what prey they consume. This evidence can help guide future conservation decisions as marine ecosystems respond to environmental change.
A model for community-led conservation
Phillip Island’s recovery story shows that successful conservation rarely happens through one dramatic action. It is usually built through many years of practical work.
The fox eradication program required rangers, farmers, scientists, government agencies, conservation organisations and local residents to work towards the same goal. Visitors also contributed through tourism, with Phillip Island Nature Parks stating that visits help fund research and wildlife conservation.
The island’s history also highlights the importance of acknowledging the Bunurong people, the Traditional Owners of Milawul. Phillip Island Nature Parks recognises the continuing connection of the Bunurong to the landscape and describes its role in healing Country and supporting Traditional Owner involvement in decisions about Country.
The little penguins’ recovery is therefore not only a story about numbers. It is a story about restoring a damaged landscape, learning from scientific evidence and changing the way people share space with wildlife.
What the future depends on
The increase from 12,000 to 40,000 little penguins is encouraging, but it does not mean the species is permanently secure on Phillip Island. Conservation gains must be maintained.
Foxes must remain absent. Other introduced predators, including feral and roaming cats, require continued management. Roads, pets, fires, rubbish, human disturbance and habitat damage can still affect wildlife.
The penguins’ time at sea also creates challenges that cannot be solved entirely on land. Their food supply may be influenced by changing ocean conditions, climate change and human activity. That is why Phillip Island’s conservation program combines population counts, breeding studies, tracking and marine research.
The lesson from Phillip Island is clear: wildlife recovery becomes possible when threats are identified early and addressed consistently. A colony that once appeared destined to vanish has grown substantially because people chose to protect its habitat, remove its predators and continue monitoring its future.
For the little penguins returning to shore each evening, that long-term commitment has made the difference between disappearance and survival.
